title: RiboBridge: protein-conditioned de novo RNA binder structure design
abstract: Designing RNA molecules that bind to target protein structures requires generating both an RNA conformation and its bound complex geometry, without assuming a predefined binding site. Existing approaches generally model these coupled processes within a unified representation, entangling RNA conformation generation with protein-relative placement. In this work, we introduce RiboBridge, a structure-first framework that separates RNA conformational generation from protein--RNA assembly through cross-frame interaction geometry. RiboBridge first proposes multiple candidate RNA-binding interfaces on the protein surface, generates canonical RNA conformations within a pretrained RNA structural latent space (RiboSphere), and then predicts protein--RNA interaction constraints to bridge the independently defined RNA and protein coordinate frames. The resulting interaction geometry is converted into a geometrically consistent protein-relative pose through rigid placement. We evaluate RiboBridge on a temporally split, sequence-filtered, and redundancy-controlled benchmark of 124 protein--RNA complexes. Under post-hoc interface-correspondence evaluation, where native information is used only after generation to select among already generated predicted-pocket candidates, RiboBridge achieves the highest fNAT and DockQ and the lowest interface and ligand RMSDs among compared methods. Component ablations and stage-wise diagnostics further characterize the contributions of RNA conformational generation, interaction prediction, and rigid placement, identifying the main sources of complex-recovery error.

title: Broad-spectrum aptamers: recent advances in selection strategies, structural mechanisms, and biosensing applications.
abstract: Broad-spectrum aptamers are single-stranded DNA or RNA molecules capable of recognizing multiple structurally or functionally related targets through adaptable molecular interactions. The increasing demand for rapid, efficient, and multi-analyte detection in complex analytical systems has exposed the limitations of conventional single-target aptamers, particularly their dependence on multiple individual recognition elements and their limited adaptability toward related analytes. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in broad-spectrum aptamers from the perspectives of target selection, structural engineering, and biosensing applications, with particular emphasis on the transition from empirical multi-target selection toward rational and mechanism-guided design. We first examine major selection strategies, including mixed-target, parallel and sequential, alternating-target, combined selection, and emerging interdisciplinary approaches, highlighting how selection pressure and target configuration influence recognition breadth, affinity, and selectivity. We then discuss structural engineering strategies, including secondary-structure regulation, chemical modification, sequence truncation and mutation, molecular simulation, and structural analysis-guided optimization, with emphasis on the molecular mechanisms underlying conformational adaptability and cross-target recognition. Recent advances in electrochemical, fluorescence, colorimetric, surface-enhanced Raman scattering, chemiluminescent, and multimodal aptasensors are further summarized, together with emerging approaches such as sensor arrays and multi-signal calibration for improving quantitative reliability in multi-analyte analysis. Finally, the major challenges and future opportunities are discussed, particularly the need to balance recognition breadth, affinity uniformity, structural adaptability, and quantitative accuracy. The integration of rational SELEX design, structural characterization, computational intelligence, nanotechnology, and miniaturized sensing platforms is expected to facilitate the development of robust, portable, and quantitatively reliable broad-spectrum aptasensors for applications in food safety, environmental monitoring, pharmaceutical analysis, and clinical diagnostics.

title: The RNA binding proteins Ddx6 and Ddx61 support development in mRNA-decay deficient pnrc2 mutants.
abstract: Somitogenesis is controlled by the segmentation clock, a molecular oscillator that controls periodic gene expression in unsegmented mesoderm and is regulated by a negative feedback loop driven by Hes/Her transcriptional repressors. In zebrafish, Pnrc2 is required for decay of her1 transcript and additional oscillatory gene transcripts. Despite accumulation of numerous mRNAs including those encoding developmental regulators, overt embryonic phenotypes are absent in pnrc2 mutants. Our previous work suggested that accumulated mRNAs are not translated in pnrc2 mutants, though the underlying mechanism(s) was unknown. We show here that many overexpressed transcripts in pnrc2 mutants have shortened poly(A) tails and are disengaged from ribosomes, and that deadenylation inhibition leads to somite defects in pnrc2 mutants. Transcripts encoding the P-body-associated protein, Ddx61, are overexpressed and engaged with ribosomes in pnrc2 mutants, leading to an increase in Ddx61 protein that may compensate against the negative effects of transcript accumulation. Co-depletion of Ddx61 and Ddx6 in pnrc2 mutants increases her1 accumulation and leads to pleiotropic defects. Together, our results show that multiple post-transcriptional mechanisms ensure proper translation when mRNA decay is inhibited.

title: Characterization of the complete mitochondrial genome of Haemaphysalis hystricis and its phylogenetic implications.
abstract: Haemaphysalis hystricis is a medically important tick vector, and three complete mitochondrial genomes derived from specimens collected from different geographic regions and hosts have previously been reported. In this study, we sequenced and analyzed the complete mitochondrial genome derived from H. hystricis specimens collected from a human host in Shaoguan, Guangdong Province, China, and systematically compared it with previously published H. hystricis mitogenomes. The complete mitogenome is 14,714 bp in length and contains 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNA genes, 2 ribosomal RNA genes, and two non-coding control regions. The overall gene order and composition are highly conserved and consistent with those reported for other Haemaphysalis species. The genome exhibits a strong A + T nucleotide bias, which is a typical feature of hard tick mitogenomes. Most tRNAs fold into typical cloverleaf secondary structures, whereas several exhibit truncated structures, reflecting a common pattern of mitochondrial tRNA structural simplification in arthropods. Selective pressure analysis indicated that all 13 PCGs are under purifying selection. Maximum-likelihood phylogenetic analysis showed that H. hystricis was most closely related to H. longicornis, consistent with previous studies. This study provides an additional H. hystricis mitogenome and compares it with the three previously published conspecific mitogenomes. The comparison revealed differences in genome length, the structure of non-coding regions, and tRNA secondary structures and provided estimates of gene-specific selective pressures. These findings provide valuable data for comparative mitogenomics and studies of intraspecific genetic variation in ticks.

title: TIA1 is required for microglial activation in tauopathy.
abstract: The RNA-binding protein T cell intracellular antigen-1 (TIA1) regulates cellular stress responses and tau pathology, key contributors to the pathophysiology of tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease (AD). TIA1 acts in peripheral monocytes to inhibit inflammation, but its function in central microglia, critical to neuroinflammation and disease progression, remains unknown. Here, we crossed TIA1 microglial conditional knockout (cKO) mice (using a Cx3cr1-driven Cre element) with the PS19 P301S MAPT mouse model of tauopathy and demonstrated that TIA1 promotes microglial activation, with a corresponding suppression of microglia activation upon TIA1cKO. We observe striking reductions in cytokine (Tnf-α and Il-1β) and sensome markers (Clec7a, Trem2, and Itgax); importantly, these reductions were accompanied by decreases in tau pathology. Proteomic analyses show TIA1 interaction with the microglial proteins C1Q, previously implicated in microglial activation. These results position TIA1 as a regulator of neuroinflammation and tauopathy in CX3CR1-expressing myeloid cells, including microglia, with potentially divergent functions in central versus peripheral immune compartments.
authors: Sophie J F van der Spek

title: In Vitro RNA Pulldown and Validation of lncRNA-Protein Interactions.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) play important roles in gene regulation and cancer progression through interactions with proteins, DNA, and other RNA molecules. Identification of lncRNA-protein interactions is therefore essential for understanding the molecular mechanisms by which lncRNAs regulate cellular processes. Among the available approaches, in vitro RNA pulldown coupled with mass spectrometry has become a widely used strategy for identifying proteins that associate with specific lncRNAs. In this chapter, we describe a detailed protocol for in vitro RNA pulldown using biotin-labeled RNA transcripts and magnetic bead capture to isolate lncRNA-binding proteins from cell lysates. We further outline complementary validation approaches, including western blot analysis, modified dot-blot assays, and RNA electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), which can be used to confirm candidate RNA-protein interactions and to map RNA-binding regions. Together, these methods provide a practical workflow for identifying and validating lncRNA-protein interactions in cancer research.

title: HuRInterDB: A Database Exploring the Landscape of lncRNA-Protein Interactions.
abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) possess diverse biological functions and play key regulatory roles in biological processes by interacting with other biomolecules, such as proteins, RNAs, and the genome. High-throughput RNA-interaction experiments have generated large volumes of lncRNA-protein interaction records. The fragmented deposition of these records across disparate public databases complicates unified retrieval and integrative analysis. Here, we present HuRInterDB (Human lncRNA-Protein Interaction Database), a comprehensive and standardized database that focuses on human lncRNA-protein interactions. HuRInterDB is a user-friendly database designed to provide an integrated resource of lncRNA-protein interaction data from 621 high-throughput datasets (encompassing 2,440,594 lncRNA-protein interactions derived from 36,184 lncRNAs and 14,888 proteins) and to support functional research on lncRNA. The web interface supports interactive searching and visualization of lncRNA-protein associations. This curated resource streamlines integrative analysis of lncRNA-protein interactions and provides a standardized foundation for future computational and experimental studies. Distinctive features include an integrated analysis module that enables interactive visualization of protein-protein interaction networks, functional word clouds, and Gene Ontology enrichment bubble plots for any queried lncRNA, as well as download functionality. HuRInterDB is freely accessible at https://nwu26-hurinterdb.share.connect.posit.cloud/, with semiannual updates and complete data downloads.

title: Oncogenic circPRRC2B regulates redox homeostasis via stabilizing TALDO1 protein of the pentose phosphate pathway in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: It remains largely unclear whether oncogenic super-enhancers (SEs) can drive expression of circular RNAs (circRNAs). In this study, we for the first time profiled the comprehensive circRNA landscapes of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) after suppressing genome-wide SE activities. We identified a novel SE-driven circPRRC2B, as the product of back-splicing of exons 2, 3, 4 and 5 of PRRC2B pre-mRNA, which was controlled by RNA binding protein HuR. Indeed, SE drives high levels of PRRC2B transcription, promotes production of PRRC2B pre-mRNAs, boosts back-splicing of PRRC2B pre-mRNAs, and elevates circPRRC2B expression. ETS1 acts as a key transcriptional factor in SE-driven PRRC2B transcription and circPRRC2B biogenesis. Interestingly, circPRRC2B, but not PRRC2B, could promote proliferation, invasion and metastasis of ESCC in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, circPRRC2B binds to TALDO1 and enhances BAP1-mediated TALDO1 de-ubiquitination in ESCC cells. Therefore, circPRRC2B stabilizes and sustains high expression of TALDO1, activates the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), elevates the glutathione levels via supplying more NADPH via the PPP, inhibits production of reactive oxygen species in mitochondrion, maintains cellular redox equilibrium, and, thus, leads to cancer progression. Importantly, we developed antisense oligonucleotides targeting circPRRC2B which exhibited remarkable inhibition of ESCC growth. Our findings highlighted circPRRC2B as a key target preserving the PPP metabolic flux and redox homeostasis of malignant cells, thereby offering insight into developing novel therapeutics for cancers.

title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
abstract: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that non-HVG handling is a central determinant of privacy: directly copying non-HVG values leads to severe leakage, whereas Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing robustness, interpretability, and privacy-conscious design choices throughout preprocessing, generation, and post-processing.

title: Pushing the boundaries of nucleic acid NMR spectroscopy.
abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy provides atomic-resolution structural information together with direct insight into nucleic acid dynamics across a wide range of timescales. Recent advances in instrumentation, isotope-labelling strategies, pulse sequence design, sensitivity enhancement and data acquisition have greatly expanded its applicability beyond small DNA and RNA systems. This review highlights how modern NMR enables the characterization of conformational ensembles, transient states and dynamic processes that are difficult to capture by other structural techniques. Particular attention is given to the integration of NMR with complementary structural and computational methods, as well as its growing application to non-canonical nucleic acid structures, large nucleic acid assemblies and studies in native cellular environments. Together, these developments have established NMR as a central tool in structural biology, bridging structure, dynamics and biological function while providing critical insights into the behaviour of nucleic acids and their interactions in health and disease.

title: Mapping programmable mRNA research relevant to cancer-associated immune escape: a dual-database bibliometric and topic modeling analysis.
abstract: Programmable messenger RNA (mRNA) platforms can encode tumor antigens or immunomodulators, enabling coordinated antigen delivery and immune modulation. Yet the literature spans cancer vaccination, delivery engineering, immune biology, and adjacent infectious-disease research, making its structure and evidentiary boundaries difficult to discern. We mapped this cross-domain corpus to clarify its development, organization, and relevance to cancer-associated immune escape. We searched the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus on July 29, 2026, for English-language Articles and Reviews published since 2006. The strategy combined programmable or therapeutic mRNA, cancer, and immune-escape-related concepts. R-based analyses summarized the number of publications (NP), total citations (TC), and collaboration patterns; BERTopic modeled titles and abstracts after entity-aware preprocessing. Independent two-author review supported the five topic labels and characterized the outliers, and robustness was assessed across alternative clustering configurations. The dataset comprised 756 publications (NP = 756). Annual output increased more than fourfold in 2021 and reached NP = 182 in 2025. China (NP = 291; 38.49%) and the United States (NP = 146; 19.31%) accounted for nearly 58% of corresponding-author publications. Sichuan University and Frontiers in Immunology ranked first in institutional and journal output, respectively. Nature had the highest retained source-record citation total (TC = 2,326). BERTopic assigned 745 publications to five topics, while 11 of 756 records remained outliers (1.46%). The topics represented mRNA delivery and immunomodulatory cancer-vaccine research (52.1%), SARS-CoV-2 vaccination in oncology and immunotherapy settings (23.6%), therapeutic mRNA cancer-vaccine platforms (13.3%), tumor-antigen discovery and immune-subtype stratification (8.6%), and mRNA-vaccine immunogenicity during autoimmune immunosuppression (2.4%). Publication activity in the retrieved cross-domain corpus expanded rapidly after 2020. The corpus included both direct cancer-mRNA research and adjacent platform or immune-response literature. By distinguishing these components and identifying thematic connections among delivery, antigen selection, immune context, and collaboration, the analysis provides an evidence-navigation framework for prioritizing systematic reviews, mechanistic studies, and clinical evaluation. The map does not itself establish therapeutic efficacy.

title: Model-based multilocus, genomic, and phenotypic integration reveals species assignment inconsistencies and sampling blind spots across Asian ecozones in Dicroglossidae.
abstract: Widespread amphibians often show inconsistent species assignments in public databases, complicating accurate range-wide biodiversity mapping and obscuring gaps in taxonomic resolution. We assessed three widespread cryptic Asian Dicroglossid genera (Fejervarya, Hoplobatrachus, Quasipaa) across Indomalayan and Palearctic ecozones, where diffuse boundaries, taxonomic uncertainty, and exotic introduction impact biodiversity patterns. Using a hierarchical, scenario-based species delimitation framework based on publicly available molecular datasets and targeted new data, we evaluated 18 species-delimitation scenarios across 14 nominal taxa, with GenBank-based assignment as a control model. All scenarios were based on shared multilocus Dicroglossidae datasets (up to 517 sequence entries), integrating GenBank data with targeted sampling across two ecozones. The best-supported scenario was further refined using genome-derived SNPs from heterogeneous data sources (GBS, RNA-seq, and WGS/WCS), together with a binary morphological trait. Across analyses, the best-supported Model A1 showed a lower MLE than GenBank-based assignments, indicating non-random taxonomic mismatches between updated local classifications and public database entries. The model delineated 17 dicroglossid clades, including a single Hoplobatrachus lineage in East Asia. Diverging over 19 Mya, Fejervarya showed pronounced cryptic structure, with two deeply divergent clades recovered within the F. limnocharis, F. kawamurai, and F. multistriata species complexes, while Quasipaa displayed deep divergences. Integration of ecological niche modelling and bioacoustic analyses for a selected sympatric pair at the ecozone boundary further showed differences in predicted habitat associations and selected acoustic traits between F. kawamurai [Clade II] and F. multistriata [Clade I], despite substantial range overlap. Fejervarya multistriata was associated with coastal lowlands, whereas F. kawamurai was more widely distributed inland. Our integrative framework highlights regions with high mismatch under dense sampling (e.g., the Yangtze-Huai transition and East Asian mainland), and regions with mismatch under limited sampling, particularly insular systems (e.g., Taiwan and Hainan), defining priorities for future genomic surveys.

title: Circular RNA Delivery In Vitro and In Vivo Using Doubly Branched Aminoethoxy-Functionalized Ionizable Lipid Nanoparticles.
abstract: Circular RNA is a therapeutically promising RNA modality with superior stability and extended protein expression relative to linear RNA. While delivery systems for linear RNA have received much attention, less effort has been directed toward the delivery of circular RNA, whose closed topology and physicochemical properties differ from those of linear RNAs. Here, we disclose a class of ionizable lipids that enable efficient in vitro and in vivo delivery of circular RNA. These ionizable lipids are step-economically accessible, allowing facile assessment of their structure-delivery relationships. Our studies reveal key elements that enhance circular RNA delivery in vitro and in vivo, including aminoethoxy head units, doubly branched tails and linkers tuned for hydrogen bonding and biodegradability. The lead ionizable lipid for circular RNA delivery, iL-19, incorporating these features, achieves ∼28-fold higher protein expression in C2C12 myocytes than Moderna's SM-102 formulation and 2.5-fold higher expression upon intramuscular administration in BALB/c mice. iL-19 also surpasses benchmark ionizable lipids ALC-0315 (7.8-fold) and DLin-MC3-DMA (33.4-fold) for intramuscular circular RNA delivery in vivo under otherwise identical conditions. This study establishes design principles and a step-economical synthesis for accessing ionizable lipids that enable highly efficient in vitro and in vivo circular RNA delivery.

title: Assessing the impact of phylogenetic reconstruction error on genetic reassortment inference in segmented viruses.
abstract: Recombination is an important process in the evolution of RNA viruses. For viruses with segmented genomes, recombination can occur by reassortment of entire genomic segments. This process has played a significant role in the adaptation and spread of influenza viruses with novel genomic combinations, i.e., antigenic shifts. Reassortment is usually identified by discrepancies between the topologies of trees reconstructed from different genomic segments, e.g., subtree prune and regraft (SPR) rearrangements. However, this phylogenetic discordance can also result from errors in tree reconstruction due to insufficient information. The objective of this study was to evaluate the contribution of phylogenetic reconstruction error to the inference of reassortment events from influenza A virus (IAV) genomes from avian hosts. We curated a dataset of 11,795 complete avian H5Nx IAV genomes and sampled subsets of HA sequences with different expected levels of reconstruction error. Next, we simulated molecular evolution along the trees reconstructed from these HA samples, varying rates of evolution and sequence lengths to correspond to the other genomic segments. Because these simulations had no reassortment, any phylogenetic discordance identified from the resulting trees must be caused by reconstruction error. We found that simulations from random samples yielded about 32% as many SPRs as obtained from real data. This false positive rate was reduced to 4% when simulating trees from the most genetically divergent subset of HA sequences. By modifying the simulated trees with SPR rearrangements, we observed a false negative rate of 8.5%, which increased with the number of SPRs per tree. Overall, we found that reassortment can be substantially overestimated from phylogenetic discordance, underscoring the need to account for phylogenetic uncertainty and sampling design when analyzing IAV datasets for reassortment.

title: Adjuvanted mucosal vaccination enhances protection and prevents influenza virus transmission in the guinea pig model.
abstract: Influenza virus infects the respiratory mucosa, highlighting the importance of mucosal immunity for early protection and transmission control. Here, we evaluated whether intranasal (IN) vaccination with recombinant trimeric hemagglutinin protein from A/Michigan/45/2015 (triHA) formulated with a combined mucosal adjuvant, nanoemulsion plus IVT, an RNA-based RIG-I agonist (NE/IVT), could protect guinea pigs against heterologous A/Netherlands/602/2009 challenge and reduce viral transmission. To compare mucosal and parenteral immunization, IN triHA/NE/IVT was benchmarked against IN triHA alone, IM triHA/AddaVax (IM triHA/Advx), and standard IM quadrivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (QIV). We also tested whether IN triHA/NE/IVT could boost IM QIV- primed immunity and included animals previously infected with A/Michigan/45/2015 to model pre-existing infection- induced immunity. Transmission was assessed by co-housing naïve sentinels with vaccinated, challenged donors. IN triHA/NE/IVT induced systemic humoral responses comparable to IM triHA/Advx while generating superior nasal mucosal IgA responses. Unexpectedly, IM triHA/AddaVax also induced detectable, albeit lower, mucosal IgG and IgA, contrasting with prior mouse data and highlighting species-specific differences. IN triHA/NE/IVT boosting after IM QIV enhanced serum IgG and mucosal IgA compared with QIV prime-boost alone and increased cross-neutralizing activity against antigenically distinct A/Victoria/4897/2022. Both IN triHA/NE/IVT and IN Michigan/15 prior- infection prevented detectable viral shedding after challenge, and naïve sentinels co-housed with IN triHA/NE/IVT- vaccinated donors remained seronegative. Together, these findings support NE/IVT as a potential mucosal platform capable of inducing robust systemic and mucosal immunity and boosting IM vaccine-primed responses.

title: Pseudouridylation landscape across 42 nuclear-encoded S. cerevisiae tRNAs.
abstract: Pseudouridine is the most abundant RNA base modification due to its prevalence in tRNA and rRNA, where it serves as a key modulator of structure and function. Yet, in the widely used model organism, the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, tRNA pseudouridine sites have not been comprehensively annotated. Here, we performed two high-throughput methods established for detecting tRNA pseudouridylation positions: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) and 2-bromoacrylamide-assisted cyclization sequencing (BACS). Using DRS, we sequenced cytosolic tRNA from seven pseudouridine synthase (PUS) knockout S. cerevisiae strains, including deletion strains of Pus1, Pus3, and Pus7. Analysis of these data verified thirty-two existing pseudouridine annotations and predicted an additional ten previously unannotated pseudouridine sites. Our analysis also revealed DRS signal changes at several non-uridine sites with the loss of a PUS, including apparent changes in modification abundances at position 37 upon deletion of Pus3. Liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and primer extension assays, however, indicated no change in the abundance of these modifications with the loss of Pus3, underscoring the need for caution in interpreting DRS-based signal changes. Using BACS, we confirmed the ten DRS-predicted novel sites, while further detecting eleven additional previously unannotated pseudouridine sites. Combining existing modification annotations from the Modomics database with our DRS and BACS datasets, we created a map of all detected pseudouridines-totaling 126 sites, including 21 novel sites-and the enzymes responsible for their catalysis, across the forty-two nuclear-encoded S. cerevisiae tRNA isoacceptors.

title: A phage-encoded small RNA that mimics chimeric guide to inhibit CRISPR-Cas9.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 relies on a dual CRISPR RNA (crRNA)-trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) guide, yet whether RNA-based anti-CRISPRs exist for this system has remained unknown. Here, we identify a phage-encoded small non-coding RNA, rAcrIIA1, that adopts an unexpected chimeric crRNA-tracrRNA architecture, faithfully recapitulating the entire single-guide RNA (sgRNA) of Cas9. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of the Cas9-rAcrIIA1 binary complex and the Cas9-rAcrIIA1-DNA ternary complex reveal that rAcrIIA1 engages Cas9 nearly identically to the native sgRNA, competitively blocking crRNA and tracrRNA loading and thereby abolishing DNA interference. Strikingly, beyond its natural inhibitory function, rAcrIIA1 is fully reprogrammable: with variable guide sequences, it directs Cas9 for sequence-specific DNA cleavage with efficiency comparable to the canonical sgRNA, and it activates trans-cleavage more potently. Thus, rAcrIIA1 provides an experimentally validated, mechanistically resolved RNA-based inhibitor of CRISPR-Cas9, reveals a distinct anti-CRISPR mechanism through complete sgRNA mimicry, and serves as a versatile bifunctional scaffold for genome editing and diagnostics.

title: Tristetraprolin attenuates microglial neuroinflammation via post-transcriptional destabilization of TRAF6 mRNA in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Microglia-driven neuroinflammation is a central pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease. Tristetraprolin (TTP), an RNA-binding protein, suppresses inflammation through facilitating the degradation of target mRNAs. However, its specific role in microglial activation during Parkinson's pathogenesis remains poorly characterized. Transcriptomic analysis was performed to identify the differentially expressed genes in A53T α-synuclein transgenic mice. TTP expression and function were assessed in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistic studies employed RNA immunoprecipitation, dual-luciferase reporter assays, and mRNA stability analyses. Therapeutic efficacy was evaluated using the NF-κB inhibitor dimethylamino parthenolide (DMAPT) in conjunction with behavioral assessments. Transcriptomic analysis revealed significant upregulation of TTP in A53T mice, accompanied by enrichment of neuroinflammatory pathways. Immunofluorescence analysis identified that increased TTP expression was mainly detected in IBA1-positive microglia. Functionally, TTP knockdown enhanced pro-inflammatory cytokine production and exacerbated primary neuronal apoptosis. Mechanistically, TTP directly bound to the 3'-untranslated region (3'UTR) of TRAF6 mRNA, accelerating its degradation and thereby suppressing TRAF6/NF-κB signaling. In vivo, TTP knockdown enhanced neuroinflammation and aggravated dopaminergic neuron loss. Pharmacological inhibition of NF-κB by DMAPT attenuated microglial activation, preserved dopaminergic neurons, and ameliorated behavioral deficits. TTP mitigated microglial neuroinflammation by promoting TRAF6 mRNA degradation and suppressing NF-κB signaling. Targeting NF-κB with DMAPT may represent a promising druggable strategy.

title: Molecular fossils of an ancestral code revealed by large-scale analysis of tRNAs.
abstract: Modern tRNAs are thought to have evolved from simpler RNA minihelices resembling acceptor stems, some of which could be specifically aminoacylated. A central and testable prediction of minihelix-based models is that vestiges of ancestral coding relationships should remain embedded within the acceptor stems of contemporary tRNAs and should persist after correction for structural constraints. Here, we ask whether cognate anticodon-like triplets are statistically enriched in nonanticodon regions of modern tRNAs beyond what would be expected from structural and compositional constraints alone. Using a curated dataset of 77,335 canonical tRNA sequences and a structure-aware statistical framework, we find that for a subset of amino acids cognate anticodon-like triplets are significantly enriched in acceptor stems and, to a lesser extent, in other structural domains. Notably, these amino acids include those previously shown to support specific minihelix aminoacylation [Y. M. Hou, P. Schimmel, Nature 333, 140-145 (1988); C. Francklyn, P. Schimmel, Nature 337, 478-481 (1989)]. The strongest acceptor-stem signals survive structure-preserving null models, and cluster nonrandomly against proposed chronologies of amino acid incorporation into the genetic code. Together, these findings identify molecular fossils within modern tRNAs consistent with the persistence of an ancestral operational code, and provide refined statistical support for the notion that extant codon-amino acid relationships evolved from early aminoacylation systems involving RNA minihelices.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: Jestvirus, a Novel Genus in the Family Autotranscriptaviridae Infecting Aeromonas.
abstract: Aeromonas species are ubiquitous, aquatic, opportunistic pathogens; however, their viral predators remain underexplored. Here, we isolated and characterized Aeromonas phage vB_AsaP_JS1, a dsDNA phage with a short non-contractile tail that infects Aeromonas salmonicida. Comparative analyses indicate that vB_AsaP_JS1 diverges from representative T7-like phages, with gene content similarity below 50% and a maximum amino acid identity of 70% or less. It forms a supported monophyletic clade in both phylogenomic and protein-based trees. Gene-sharing network analysis further shows that vB_AsaP_JS1 and its closest relatives form a distinct, isolated cluster, clearly separated from all currently recognized genera within the family Autotranscriptaviridae and related lineages of Caudoviricetes. Collectively, these features satisfy ICTV criteria for genus demarcation and support the establishment of a novel phage genus, tentatively designated Jestvirus. Functional annotation highlights a compact transcriptional module containing a single-subunit T7-like RNA polymerase and a streamlined replication packaging operon. Several putative host-interaction-related genes, including a deoxycytidine kinase homolog, a PelC-like protein, and a putative glycosidase, are encoded in the genome; their possible roles in nucleotide scavenging or host interaction during infection represent hypotheses that require experimental validation. Metagenomic read mapping reveals sequence-level signals related to vB_AsaP_JS1 in wastewater datasets from multiple geographic regions, suggesting a potentially wider environmental distribution for this phage lineage than previously recognized, though confirmation of phage identity and prevalence will require further investigation. Together, our results expand the known genomic diversity of T7-like phages and provide taxonomic, functional, and ecological evidence for a new phage lineage within Caudoviricetes.

title: Nitrogen-Functionalized Amphilectane-Type Diterpenoids with Anti-HBV Activity from the Okinawan Marine Sponge Stylissa sp.
abstract: Current treatments for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection are constrained by adverse effects, drug resistance, and the need for long-term administration. Therefore, the development of safer and more effective therapeutic agents remains an important priority. In this study, two new amphilectane-type diterpenoids, 7-isocyanatoneoamphilecta-11,15-diene (1) and 7-isothiocyanatoneoamphilecta-11,15-diene (2), together with three known analogues (3-5), were isolated as anti-HBV agents from the Okinawan marine sponge Stylissa sp. The structures of 1 and 2 were elucidated by spectroscopic analysis, single-crystal X-ray diffraction, microcrystal electron diffraction (microED), and chemical derivatization. The previously reported amphilectanes 6 and 7 from an Adociidae sponge were also evaluated to examine structure-activity relationships. Compounds 3 and 6 showed the most potent anti-HBV activity and significantly suppressed the formation of HBV covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) without affecting HBV binding, entry, or RNA transcription. These results suggest that the combination of an isocyanide group and an exomethylene moiety is critical for activity. This study expands the chemical diversity of amphilectane diterpenoids and highlights their potential as promising scaffolds for the development of anti-HBV therapeutics.

title: Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains.
abstract: Over the past 5 to 7 million years, humans and chimpanzees have diverged in brain size, structure, and cognition despite high conservation of protein-coding genes. However, retroviral infections within host genomes have introduced numerous species-specific regulatory elements. Chimpanzees harbor lineage-specific PTERV1 endogenous retroviruses that are absent in humans, but their role in brain evolution has remained unclear. We performed an epigenomic analysis of PTERV1 insertions in chimpanzee neural organoids and found they are heavily DNA methylated, forming over 150 species-specific heterochromatin domains with the potential to influence gene regulation. We identified a chimpanzee-specific insertion on chromosome 19 that silences the long noncoding RNA LINC00662 through DNA methylation spreading. CRISPR-mediated deletion of this PTERV1 restored LINC00662 expression in chimpanzee induced pluripotent stem cells. We show that LINC00662, a human-specific transcript expressed during brain development, plays a role in neuronal maturation, axon outgrowth, and neural organoid development. These findings reveal a mechanism by which endogenous retroviral insertions contributed to human-chimpanzee brain divergence.

title: Opposing cell-type preferences for binding and replication shape influenza A virus infection in human airways.
abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAVs) pose a threat to human health. Although receptor specificity, polymerase adaptation, and airway tropism have been studied extensively, it remains unresolved how they combine to shape tropism in airway epithelia. Here, we show that avian IAVs infect ciliated and secretory cells but preferentially bind to ciliated cells because of higher apical α2,3-linked sialic acid levels. As replication levels are comparable between cell types, this translates into overall preference for ciliated cells. Human IAVs also preferentially bind to ciliated cells despite comparable α2,6-linked sialic acid abundance. Instead, they show higher viral RNA and protein levels in secretory cells, linked to their compatibility with human ANP32 proteins and modestly higher ANP32A/B expression in this cell type, resulting in equal infection levels across cell types. Our findings redefine IAV tropism in the human airway as a stage-resolved process shaped by the interplay between apical glycans, viral binding, polymerase cofactor compatibility, and cell-type-specific replication capacity, moving beyond receptor-centric models.

title: In situ CAR-M engineered by liposomal mRNA nanomedicine remodels fibrotic microenvironment for ameliorating liver fibrosis.
abstract: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)-incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)-CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.

title: MARS-RNA: An Automated Pipeline for Correlating RNA Molecular Dynamics Trajectories with Chemical Probing Data.
abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules fold into complex, highly dynamic three-dimensional conformational structures that govern their biological activities. Chemical probing methods, such as SHAPE (selective 2'-hydroxyl acylation analyzed by primer extension), provide structural insights in the form of one-dimensional (1D) nucleotide reactivity profiles. However, mapping these one-dimensional profiles back to the underlying dynamic structures remains a key challenge, as traditional analyses rely on a static view based on three-dimensional (3D) high-resolution structures from X-ray crystallography or nuclear magnetic resonance, rather than accounting for the dynamic nature of the system. In this Application Note, we introduce MARS-RNA (Molecular dynamics Analysis for Reactivity and Structure), an automated pipeline that extracts and integrates multiscale structural and geometric features from RNA Molecular Dynamics (MD) trajectories, combining them with secondary (2D) and 3D annotations from X3DNA-DSSR to identify features that correlate with experimental reactivity. MARS-RNA processes raw GROMACS trajectories, performs frame-by-frame structural annotation, calculates spatial centroids and physical distance fluctuations, computes Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficients against SHAPE data, and preprocesses results for machine learning pipelines. We show its value on the RNA 3'-UTR (PDB ID: 1AUD, chain A), by highlighting several single correlation with SHAPE reactivity.

title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis.
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

title: METTL3-METTL14 Heterodimer Assembly Enables Multivalent RNA Engagement and Is Tuned by Interface-Targeting Peptides.
abstract: RNA N6-methyladenosine (m6A) deposition by the METTL3-METTL14 complex regulates RNA metabolism and thereby influences cell differentiation and stress responses. Dysregulated m6A deposition has been implicated in multiple cancers, where METTL3-METTL14 supports oncogenic programs. Yet the molecular basis of RNA recognition by this complex remains unclear, in part due to the lack of an RNA-bound structure of the full assembly. Here, we combined native mass spectrometry (MS), molecular modeling, biochemical assays, and cell-based studies to define how METTL3-METTL14 engages RNA and how this process can be perturbed through interface targeting. Native MS of the intact heterodimer revealed simultaneous binding of multiple RNA molecules, with RNA-dependent stoichiometries and higher-occupancy states consistent with cooperative interactions. Molecular dynamics simulations identified a structured RNA-bound assembly in which the METTL14 C-terminal RGG-rich region stabilizes two RNA molecules, supporting a pre-engaged substrate configuration. We further developed a focused library of METTL14-derived peptides that bind METTL3 and interfere with protein-protein interactions, identifying the minimal METTL14 epitope for interface engagement. The most potent peptide, R8-14, binds with submicromolar affinity, disrupts both METTL3-METTL14 association and higher-order RNA-bound states, and reduces m6A levels, c-Myc expression, and cancer cell viability. Together, these findings demonstrate that RNA recognition by METTL3-METTL14 is governed by multivalent, higher-order interactions that enhance binding avidity. Notably, this assembly can be perturbed allosterically through protein-protein interface targeting rather than active-site inhibition, highlighting multivalent RNA recognition as a mechanistically and pharmacologically actionable feature of the RNA m6A writer complex.

title: Hippo Pathway Modulation Alters the Proteome and Migratory Phenotype of Prostate Cancer Cells.
abstract: The Hippo pathway effector YAP1 has been implicated in prostate cancer progression, migration, and castration resistance, yet how pharmacological YAP1 inhibition reshapes the prostate cancer proteome remains uncharacterized. We used label-free quantitative proteomics together with functional assays to characterize the proteomic and phenotypic effects of CA3, a selective YAP1 inhibitor, in androgen-independent PC3 and androgen-sensitive LNCaP prostate cancer cells, and validated key findings with wound-healing, western blot, and immunodetection assays for focal adhesion kinase (FAK), vimentin, occludin, and junctional adhesion molecule A (JAM-A). CA3 reduced cell viability and YAP1 protein levels in both cell lines in a dose- and time-dependent manner (p < 0.05). Nonlinear regression analysis yielded 24 h IC50 values of 1.59 µM (95% CI, 1.38-1.83) for PC3 and 0.63 µM (95% CI, 0.53-0.77) for LNCaP, with corresponding 48 h values of 0.59 µM (95% CI, 0.50-0.69) and 0.49 µM (95% CI, 0.39-0.62). CA3 showed markedly lower potency in the non-tumorigenic PNT1A prostate epithelial cell line (IC50 18.87 µM at 24 h; 4.47 µM at 48 h), corresponding to an approximately 7- to 30-fold selectivity window favoring the cancer cell lines. Label-free quantitative proteomics identified 365 and 153 differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in PC3 and LNCaP cells, respectively. Functional enrichment analysis revealed cell line-dependent alterations in pathways related to RNA metabolism and translation, alongside migration- and adhesion-associated processes, including focal adhesion, cytoskeletal organization, and guidance signaling. Comparison of these proteins with the Gene Ontology cell migration gene set (GO:0016477) identified EGFR, SRC, TGFB1, IL6, and SCARB1 as hub proteins in PC3 cells, and RAC1, RHOC, NF1, FSCN1, and ASPM in LNCaP cells. Functional validation confirmed that CA3 reduced wound closure in both cell lines, decreased FAK protein levels, selectively reduced vimentin in PC3 cells, increased occludin in both cell lines, and increased JAM-A specifically in PC3 cells (all p < 0.05). To our knowledge, this is the first study to characterize the CA3-induced proteome in prostate cancer cells and link these changes to migration-associated protein networks, in cell lines with differing androgen dependence.

title: Impairing Golgin-45 transcription factor activity unleashes malignant secretion in lung cancer.
abstract: Golgin-45 (G45) is a coiled-coil protein that transits reversibly between the Golgi and nucleus. In the Golgi, G45 serves as a tether for effectors of a pro-tumorigenic secretory program, but its nuclear role remains unclear. Here, we report that, upon entering the nucleus, G45 functions as a basic leucine zipper transcription factor. From genomic mapping, RNA-sequencing, and functional validation studies, we identify G45-binding sites and show that nuclear G45 can function as a transcriptional activator or repressor, a versatility enabled by phase separation into nuclear bodies enriched in transcriptional co-regulators. In lung cancer models, Golgi-docking reinforces, whereas nuclear translocation opposes, pro-tumorigenic activity of G45. Nuclear G45 incorporates into dimeric transcription factors that silence pro-tumorigenic secreted cargos. Epigenetic events in lung cancer degrade nuclear G45 and sequester G45 in the Golgi, which unleashes malignant secretion. Thus, inter-organelle transitions govern a G45-dependent secretory axis that drives lung cancer progression.

title: Purification of RNA G-Quadruplex Binding Proteins.
abstract: G-quadruplex (G4) nucleic acids have been shown to regulate a wide range of cellular processes, including replication, telomere maintenance, epigenetic landscape, and various aspects of transcription and translation. In this method, we describe an experimental purification procedure for identifying RNA G-quadruplex-binding proteins from nuclear extracts. Using biotinylated oligonucleotides allows immobilization to streptavidin-coated magnetic beads and convenient washing during the pulldown. Importantly, the experimental protocol presented here can distinguish protein interactions with structured and unstructured RNA within the same oligonucleotide by controlling ionic conditions throughout the folding, RNA pulldown, and washing steps. The binding of individual candidate proteins can be determined by western blotting, while mass spectrometry can readily identify the whole RNA G-quadruplex-interacting proteome.

title: Purification of Nascent, Chromatin-Associated RNA Enriched for RNA Modifications.
abstract: RNAs that are being synthesized and remain tethered to chromatin during transcription are key participants in co-transcriptional gene regulation. They contribute to essential processes such as splicing, transcription elongation, and chromatin structure shaping. Co- and post-transcriptional RNA modifications have emerged as critical regulators of RNA metabolism and may modulate the function of chromatin-associated RNAs, including their interactions with chromatin. Here, we describe a method to isolate nascent, chromatin-associated RNA enriched for specific RNA modifications, using a combination of metabolic labeling, cell fractionation, and immunoprecipitation. This approach involves labeling of newly transcribed RNA with nucleotide analogs, followed by subcellular fractionation to enrich for chromatin-bound RNA species. Subsequently, immunoprecipitation with RNA modification-specific antibodies is used to selectively purify RNA bearing specific epitranscriptomic marks. We detail each component of the protocol, which can be adapted to various mammalian cell types and experimental conditions. The nature of this workflow enables investigation of RNA modifications on nascent, chromatin-associated transcripts under physiological or perturbed conditions, including various stimuli, genetic mutants, or disease-relevant cell lines.

title: TLR8 gain-of-function syndrome.
abstract: Toll-like receptor 8 (TLR8) is an endosomal pattern recognition receptor highly expressed in myeloid cells that senses RNA degradation fragments. Monogenic gain-of-function (GOF) variants in TLR8 cause an inborn error of immunity (IEI) with a spectrum of immune-mediated pathology ranging from severe lymphoproliferation with neutropenia and bone marrow failure to anemia and autoimmunity. Half of identified patients have mosaic disease-causing variants, with variant allele fractions as low as 7% sufficient to drive systemic immune dysregulation. This, along with immunologic profiling of patients, demonstrates a dominant mechanism of disease, likely mediated by inflammatory cytokines. Disease-causing variants in TLR8 are enriched at or near agonist and antagonist binding sites in the encoded protein. As a spectrum of disease and genotypes emerges, identifying sensitivity to agonism and resistance to antagonism may provide insight into molecular mechanisms and therapeutic targets. Here, we review the genetics and clinical features of 19 reported cases of TLR8 GOF diseases, and future areas of investigation for this IEI.

title: Atypical E3 ligase HOIL1 promotes MDA5 signaling and ester-linked ubiquitination of LGP2.
abstract: The RIG-I-like receptors, RIG-I and MDA5, are innate sensors of RNA virus infections that are critical for mounting a robust antiviral immune response. Heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1), a component of the linear ubiquitin chain assembly complex (LUBAC), is essential for interferon induction in response to viruses sensed by MDA5, but not viruses sensed by RIG-I; however, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. LUBAC contains two atypical E3 ubiquitin ligases, HOIL1 and HOIP. While HOIP generates "linear" polyubiquitin chains, HOIL1 catalyzes ester-linked ubiquitination of serine and threonine residues and glucosaccharides. Here, we show that HOIL1 E3 ligase activity is critical for MDA5-dependent interferon induction, whereas HOIP E3 ligase activity plays a minor role. Mechanistically, HOIL1 E3 ligase activity was required for MDA5 translocation to mitochondrion-associated membranes and the formation of MAVS aggregates. We further identified LGP2, a positive regulator of MDA5 oligomerization, as a HOIL1-interacting protein and substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination. In mice, loss of HOIL1 or its E3 ligase activity markedly impaired early interferon responses following infection with viruses sensed by MDA5. While HOIL1 deficiency resulted in increased viral burden and reduced survival, loss of HOIL1 ligase activity alone did not, indicating that HOIL1 exerts additional functions during antiviral immunity. Collectively, these findings establish ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1 as a critical mechanism regulating MDA5 signaling.IMPORTANCEThe rapid and robust production of interferon is critical for controlling viral infections. Cytoplasmic RNA sensors, RIG-I and MDA5, detect infection with distinct groups of viruses, leading to the transcriptional induction of interferon. However, inappropriate production of interferon triggered by aberrant MDA5 activation by cellular RNAs causes severe inflammatory disorders. Here, we report that the ubiquitin ligase activity of heme-oxidized IRP2 ligase 1 (HOIL1) is critical for the production of interferon in response to viruses that are sensed by MDA5 in cells and mice. We identify the third RIG-I-like receptor, LGP2, as a substrate for ester-linked ubiquitination by HOIL1, and show that, like LGP2, HOIL1 ubiquitin ligase activity is required for the efficient oligomerization of MDA5 and the initiation of downstream signaling leading to the induction of interferon. These findings reveal a new regulator of MDA5-driven interferon production and identify a potential therapeutic target for MDA5-mediated inflammatory diseases.

title: LncRNA ZFPM2 silencing alleviates lung epithelial injury by inducing M2 macrophage polarization: possible implication in bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
abstract: To screen the key long-chain non-coding RNA (LncRNA) closely related to the occurrence and development of Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and explore its mechanism of affecting lung epithelial cell injury. Based on the BPD mouse model induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), LncRNA high-throughput sequencing was used to screen differentially expressed LncRNAs. GO and KEGG functional enrichment analysis were performed on differentially expressed target genes. The expressions of key LncRNA in LPS-induced MLE-12 and MH-S cells were verified. ZFPM2 specific siRNA (si-ZFPM2) and negative control (si-NC) plasmids were transfected into LPS-induced cells. Cells were divided into control group, LPS group, LPS + si-NC group, and LPS + si-ZFPM2 group. Cell vitality was measured by CCK-8 method, pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, IL-4) were quantified, and M1 (iNOS, CD86) and M2 (CD206, Arg1) markers were detected. In MLE-12 cells, cell apoptosis rate was further detected, and the protein expressions of NLRP3 and caspase-1 were analysed. A Transwell co-culture system was established with MH-S cells in the upper chamber (treated as above) and MLE-12 cells in the lower chamber; the latter were harvested to assess viability, apoptosis, NLRP3/caspase-1 expression, and inflammatory cytokine levels. A total of 1,290 differentially expressed LncRNAs and 4,084 differentially expressed mRNAs were screened by LncRNA sequencing. Functional enrichment analysis showed that these differential genes were closely related to the development of lung epithelial cells and macrophage polarization. The expression of ZFPM2 was markedly upregulated in BPD mouse lung tissue and in LPS-stimulated cells. In MH-S cells, silencing ZFPM2 significantly increased cell viability, decreased M1 markers (iNOS, CD86) and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), and increased M2 markers (CD206, Arg1) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-4, IL-10). In MLE-12 cells, silencing ZFPM2 significantly improved viability, reduced apoptosis, and suppressed NLRP3/caspase-1 protein expression and IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α levels. In the co-culture system, silencing ZFPM2 significantly enhanced MLE-12 viability, reduced apoptosis and NLRP3/caspase-1 expression, lowered pro-inflammatory cytokines, and elevated anti-inflammatory cytokines. Silencing ZFPM2 can alleviate LPS-induced injury of pulmonary epithelial cells, which may be related to promoting the polarization of alveolar macrophages towards M2 type and inhibiting inflammatory response.

title: Artificial intelligence and biotechnology for smart storage: Quality and safety perspectives in horticultural produce.
abstract: Addressing the global challenge of postharvest losses in horticultural produce requires the continuous development of innovative strategies that integrate cutting-edge technology with fundamental biological knowledge. This review explores the synergy between artificial intelligence (AI), biotechnology, and traditional postharvest management strategies to improve the quality, safety, and shelf-life of fruits and vegetables (F&V). We examine the physiological and molecular mechanisms driving postharvest deterioration, including respiration, senescence, and host-pathogen interactions, while evaluating how AI-driven tools are advancing quality monitoring, predictive analytics, and supply chain optimization. Furthermore, we assess the potential of advanced biotechnological interventions, such as CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and RNA interference techniques, to extend shelf-life and enhance the disease resistance in horticultural crops. By evaluating recent progress in these domains, we present integrated strategies that combine biological insight with digital transformation for sustainable postharvest management. The effective implementation of these approaches holds considerable potential to reduce F&V waste, enhance food security, and create horticultural supply chains that are more resilient to ever growing global production and evolving environmental challenges.

title: The complete chloroplast genome data of Bergera glabra (Guillaumin) F.J.Mou, a potential aromatic plant endemic to Vietnam.
abstract: The genus Bergera J.Koenig is renowned for the curry tree (Bergera koenigii L.) and related aromatic species. However, most available genomic data for this genus have focused on B. koenigii because of its widespread use as a spice. In this study, we sequence and report the complete chloroplast genome of Bergera glabra (Guillaumin) F.J.Mou, a species endemic to Vietnam. The reported genome has a quadripartite structure, comprising a large single-copy region (87,759 bp and 37.1% GC), a small single-copy region (18,075 bp and 33.7% GC), and two inverted repeat regions (27,112 bp and 43% GC each). Additionally, the genome contains 79 protein-coding genes, 30 transfer RNA genes, and four ribosomal RNA genes. Phylogenetic analysis indicated the monophyly of the genus Bergera and a close relationship between B. glabra and Bergera euchrestifolia (Hayata) F.J.Mou. This study expands the genomic data of the genus Bergera and provides useful information for further genomic studies examining population genetics and molecular markers for B. glabra and other related Bergera taxa.

title: Identification of small-molecule inhibitors of the immune system repressor Regnase-1.
abstract: Regnase-1 is an essential RNase that suppresses immune cell activation by targeting the mRNA of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin 6 (IL-6). Although genetic inhibition of Regnase-1 activity in CD8+ T cells has been shown to enhance antitumor immunity, no molecular inhibitors of Regnase-1 have been reported. By exploiting a library of nucleic acid analogs in conjunction with an RNA displacement assay, we identified multiple candidate competitors of Regnase-1 RNA substrates. Among these, suramin-an approved drug for treating African sleeping sickness-and several of its derivatives displaced Regnase-1 RNA targets with submicromolar affinity, competitively inhibited Regnase-1-mediated degradation of RNA in vitro, and enhanced Il6 mRNA levels and IL-6 production in mouse embryonic fibroblasts. A 2.62 Å crystal structure revealed that suramin bound to the Regnase-1 active site, coordinating with the catalytic Mg2+. Quantum chemical calculations further elucidated qualitative interactions between suramin and surrounding residues of Regnase-1. These findings establish suramin as a small-molecule inhibitor of Regnase-1-mediated RNA decay.

title: Comparative organelle genome analysis of three medicinal species of the genus Woodwardia (Blechnaceae): new insights into the phylogeny and molecular identification.
abstract: Plants of the genus Woodwardia have a long history of medicinal use in China. Among these plants, Woodwardia japonica, Woodwardia unigemmata, and Woodwardia prolifera are the primary source species of Guan Zhong, a traditional Chinese medicine. However, because of morphological similarity among their dried herbal materials and limited availability of organellar (mitochondrial and chloroplast) genomic data, research on species identification, molecular evolution, and phylogeny has been impeded. Organelle genomes of the three Woodwardia species were sequenced and assembled using the second- and third-generation sequencing technologies. In-depth analyses were conducted, including protein-coding genes (PCGs) presence/absence, non-synonymous/synonymous mutation ratios (Ka/Ks), codon usage bias, repeat sequence identification, RNA editing site prediction, synteny and mitochondrial-chloroplast homologous fragment (MTPT) identification, and molecular identification via mVISTA and nucleotide diversity. Finally, we employed both maximum likelihood (ML) and Bayesian (BI) methods, based on single-copy orthologous genes and secondary calibrations, to infer phylogenetic relationships and divergence times among Woodwardia and related ferns. The mitochondrial genomes of the three Woodwardia species exhibited notable differences in genome size and characteristics; while the chloroplast genomes were relatively conserved and highly similar. Phylogenetic and divergence time analyses indicated that W. unigemmata and W. prolifera are more closely related and diverged more recently. Integrated analyses of highly variable regions and phylogenetic revealed that the intergenic spacer rrn16-rps12_exon2 or rps12_exon2-rrn16 could effectively differentiate the three Guan Zhong-related Woodwardia species, suggesting their potential utility as reliable DNA barcodes for identifying medicinal materials. The results provide comprehensive insights and reliable, detailed organelle genomic data for the phylogeny and molecular identification of W. japonica, W. unigemmata, and W. prolifera.

title: High-dose capsaicin exposure is associated with more severe inflammation, intestinal dysregulation, and IL-17 elevation in experimental autoimmune uveitis.
abstract: To investigate whether capsaicin exposure increases the severity of experimental autoimmune uveitis (EAU) and to further characterize the associated alterations in intestinal homeostasis and immune regulation. Mice were orally administered different doses of capsaicin (CAP) from the day of EAU induction through the peak of disease on day 21. EAU severity was evaluated by fundus imaging, clinical scoring, and retinal histopathological scoring. Intestinal morphological changes were assessed by hematoxylin and eosin staining, while intestinal barrier integrity was evaluated by detecting colonic ZO-1 and MUC2 expression using immunofluorescence staining and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. IL-17A levels in the colon and spleen were quantified by ELISA. Fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, untargeted metabolomics, and colonic RNA sequencing were performed to characterize alterations in gut microbiota, metabolic profiles, and inflammatory pathways. Based on the identification of reduced kynurenic acid (KYNA) levels, KYNA co-treatment was subsequently performed to evaluate its effects on ocular inflammation, IL-17A levels, and intestinal barrier-related alterations during high-dose CAP exposure. In the 80 mg/kg CAP group, retinal inflammation and tissue injury were more pronounced than in the other groups, accompanied by higher clinical and histopathological scores and increased IL-17A levels in the colon and spleen. High-dose CAP was also associated with ileal architectural abnormalities, reduced colonic mucosal thickness, and decreased colonic ZO-1 and MUC2 expression. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed alterations in gut microbial diversity and community structure. CAP-associated differential metabolites were enriched in the tryptophan metabolism pathway, and fecal KYNA levels were significantly reduced. KEGG over-representation analysis identified significant enrichment of the IL-17 signaling pathway among CAP-upregulated genes, whereas GSEA was not significant after multiple-testing correction, upregulation of Il17a, Il17f, and Rorc, and altered expression of genes involved in tryptophan metabolism. KYNA co-treatment reduced clinical and histopathologic scores, decreased IL-17A levels in the colon and spleen, and partially restored colonic ZO-1 and MUC2 expression. High-dose CAP exposure during EAU induction was associated with increased disease severity, accompanied by disrupted intestinal homeostasis, reduced fecal KYNA levels, and enhanced IL-17-related inflammation. KYNA co-treatment partially attenuated CAP-associated ocular and intestinal alterations.

title: Research progress in gene editing of Brassicaceae crops.
abstract: Brassicaceae crops are globally important economic plants, whose yield and quality directly affect the supply of edible oil and vegetables. Most of these crops are polyploids with complex genomes and numerous homoeologous gene copies, which demand high efficiency and specificity from gene editing tools, while providing ideal models for studying the rules of polyploid genome editing. Traditional breeding methods, such as crossbreeding and mutation breeding, are constrained by long cycles, low efficiency, and poor specificity, making them insufficient for precise genetic improvement. Gene editing technologies, characterized by precision, efficiency, and targeting specific genomic loci, are core tools for crop breeding. Among these, ZFNs and TALENs rely on protein-DNA recognition and are complicated and costly to design; CRISPR-Cas, which achieves precise recognition through base pairing between guide RNA and target DNA, is simple, efficient, and the most widely used editing tool. Base and prime editors enable single-nucleotide substitutions or small fragment insertions without generating double-strand breaks, making them suitable for directed modification of point mutations. This review summarizes the progress of gene editing in Brassicaceae for bolting/flowering, plant architecture, nutritional quality, tolerance to abiotic stresses (temperature, salinity, drought, heavy metals), and resistance to biotic stresses (diseases, pests). We analyze challenges, including off-target effects, difficulties in polyploid genome editing, and imperfect genetic transformation systems, and discuss future directions integrating gene editing with multi-omics and artificial intelligence. This review aims to provide a theoretical basis and technical support for precise molecular breeding of Brassicaceae crops.

title: Sequence-activity mapping and model-guided engineering of the phenol-responsive DmpR-Po σ54 promoter.
abstract: Promoters are core cis-regulatory elements that determine gene expression levels and dynamic responses, and their quantitative engineering directly dictates the performance of synthetic biological systems such as whole-cell biosensors. However, the transcriptional output of complex inducible systems, exemplified by σ54-dependent promoters, relies on long-range coordination among distal bacterial enhancer-binding proteins, DNA architectural proteins, and RNA polymerase. The combined effects of multiple regulatory regions on promoter output remain poorly understood, which limits the cross-background transfer of local sequence rules and hinders the accurate prediction and rational design of promoter activity. The phenol-responsive DmpR-Po promoter serves as both a classical model for investigating σ54-dependent regulation and a high-value sensing element for environmental pollutant detection and high-throughput enzyme activity screening. Resolving sequence-activity relationships across its complete regulatory region therefore holds both mechanistic and practical significance. To overcome the barriers to rational engineering of complex promoters, we established a modular design-measure-model-guide-validate framework targeting the full DmpR-Po regulatory region. A library of 17,500 designed promoter sequences was constructed to systematically perturb the upstream activating sequence (UAS), the IHF2 region, combined UAS-IHF2 mutational backgrounds, and downstream regulatory architecture. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting coupled with sequencing yielded a high-quality sequence-activity map covering 11,940 variants. At the regional level, identical UAS and IHF2 haplotypes generally preserved their relative activity rankings across single-region and joint-variant backgrounds, and the main effects estimated independently for UAS and IHF2 could approximately predict the activity of combined variants. At the nucleotide level, however, the effects of individual substitutions were strongly constrained by the overall DNA architecture and full-sequence context. A deep learning model trained on the complete regulatory sequence captured these context-dependent relationships, achieved robust predictive performance on held-out sequences and a separately transformed and processed Batch 2 derived from the same preconstructed plasmid-library pool, and enabled model-guided prioritization of targeted local variants. Single-clone validation further showed that model-guided edits produced variable experimental outcomes, supporting candidate prioritization while indicating that individual engineering predictions require experimental validation. Collectively, this study characterizes the transferability and context-dependent constraints of regional sequence effects and establishes a data-driven framework for quantitative prediction and model-guided engineering of complex σ54-dependent promoters.

title: Hyaluronan-Mediated Motility Receptor Potentiates Colorectal Carcinoma Progression Through PI3K/AKT/mTOR Pathway Modulation.
abstract: This study aimed to interrogate the functional role of hyaluronan-mediated motility receptor (HMMR) in modulating proliferative, migratory, and invasive phenotypes of colorectal cancer (CRC) cells, with an emphasis on its relationship with the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling cascade. Protein expression levels of HMMR and components of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway were comparatively analyzed in an exploratory paired tissue series of colorectal tumors and adjacent non-neoplastic tissues (n = 5) via Western blotting and immunohistochemistry. Functional perturbation was achieved through RNA interference and plasmid-mediated overexpression of HMMR in HCT-15 cells. Cellular behaviors were quantitatively assessed using Cell Counting Kit-8 viability assays, flow cytometric analysis of cell cycle distribution, and motility/invasion assays. The functional involvement of the PI3K pathway was examined through fixed-dose pharmacological modulation using an inhibitor and an agonist. HMMR expression was elevated in the paired CRC tissues relative to adjacent controls, accompanied by increased phosphorylation of PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway components. Silencing of HMMR significantly reduced HCT-15 cell viability over a 24-72 h interval (p < 0.01), induced G1-phase arrest (p < 0.05), and attenuated migratory and invasive phenotypes (p < 0.01), whereas ectopic HMMR expression produced the opposite pattern. Pharmacological pathway modulation attenuated or partially rescued HMMR-associated phenotypes, supporting functional involvement of PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling. Within the experimental scope of this study, HMMR acts as a functional contributor to malignant phenotypes in HCT-15 CRC cells and is associated with PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway activation. These findings support a mechanistic relationship between HMMR expression and pathway activity without establishing a direct physical interaction between HMMR and individual pathway proteins.

title: PPR9 mediates mitochondrial nad transcript maturation required for complex I biogenesis and early plant development in Arabidopsis.
abstract: The biogenesis and function of plant mitochondria relies on the expression of the organellar genome, which involves extensive post-transcriptional processing of organellar transcripts in order to generate mature functional RNAs. This includes the removal of introns from many essential organellar transcripts through splicing, a process mediated by diverse nuclear-encoded RNA-processing factors, including numerous members of the pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) protein family. Here, we report the analysis of PPR9 (At1g03560), a mitochondrial P-class PPR protein originally identified in genetic screens for essential protein cofactors. Loss of PPR9 function results in embryonic arrest at early stages of seed development. In vitro rescued homozygous ppr9 mutant plants could be recovered and maintained using a modified in vitro embryo-rescue method. The mutants display delayed growth and development which are associated with altered mitochondrial functions. Molecular analyses reveal that PPR9 functions in the splicing of several mitochondrial transcripts encoding respiratory complex I (CI) subunits, including nad2 intron 3 and nad7 introns 1 and 2. Accordingly, CI assembly is disrupted in ppr9 plants, resulting in altered OXPHOS activity and broad physiological defects. Together, these findings identify PPR9 as a key regulator of mt-RNA maturation in Arabidopsis, enabling CI biogenesis and optimal respiratory functions, and further highlight the roles of nuclear-encoded factors in coordinating mitochondria functions and (early) plant growth and development.

title: DZIP3 is a viral RNA co-sensor for RIG-I that promotes type-I interferon responses.
abstract: RNA-binding E3 ubiquitin ligases have the ability to link RNA regulation to the protein ubiquitination machinery, thereby influencing diverse biological processes. Here, we identify the RNA-binding E3 ubiquitin ligase DZIP3 as an innate immune sensor that couples viral RNA recognition to downstream immune signaling. Upon viral infection, binding of viral RNA to the DZIP3 RNA-binding motif induces conformational changes that promote K63-linked auto-ubiquitination, oligomerization, and stabilization of DZIP3. Activated DZIP3 associates with RIG-I and MAVS at the mitochondrial membrane, promoting K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I and robust activation of the type-I interferon response. Consequently, DZIP3 depletion impairs host antiviral defense, whereas DZIP3 restricts infection by a broad range of RNA viruses. Our findings establish DZIP3 as an innate immune co-sensor that integrates viral RNA detection with ubiquitin-mediated signaling, revealing a regulatory mechanism of RIG-I-MAVS-mediated antiviral immunity.

title: A phage DUF669 protein mediates post-cleavage DNA repair against host CRISPR immunity.
abstract: Phages have evolved various anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins or RNA-based anti-CRISPR (Racr) to evade host CRISPR immunity by direct interference. However, whether other counter-CRISPR mechanisms exist remains unexplored. Here, we report a phage-encoded two-protein system, termed Healer, which neutralizes CRISPR immunity via a post-cleavage DNA repair mechanism. This phage replication-associated system comprises two proteins: Gp63 (a DUF669 domain-containing protein), and Gp64 (an AAA domain-containing protein). Mechanistic investigations elucidate that Gp63 acts as a rapid-response effector of CRISPR-induced DNA breaks. After Gp63 binds ssDNA, it promotes Gp64-mediated homologous recombination, which repairs CRISPR-generated phage DNA breaks and supports phage viability.
