Notably, co-expression of the Healer system with Cas9/Cas12 in E. coli, P. aeruginosa, and A. baumannii demonstrated high phage genome-editing efficiency. Collectively, our findings reveal an important anti-CRISPR complementary strategy, providing a promising tool for genome engineering.

title: Rubicon modulates neuroimmune responses following traumatic brain injury.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) elicits robust neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, coupled with an acute inhibition of macro-autophagy (autophagy) in neurons and microglia. Rubicon (Rubcn), a Beclin1 interacting protein that suppresses autophagy and mediates LC3-associated phagocytosis and endocytosis (LAP/LANDO), influences inflammatory signaling in metabolic, neurodegenerative, and inflammaging diseases; yet its role in acquired brain injury has not been examined. Using a controlled cortical impact model, we investigated the role of Rubicon in acute neuroinflammatory responses following injury by comparing wild-type and Rubcn-mutant mice. Bulk-RNA sequencing of injured cortex revealed attenuated induction of inflammatory pathways and reduced activation of pro-inflammatory microglial/macrophage phenotype in injured Rubcn-mutant mice. Rubcn-mutant mice demonstrated less pronounced inhibition of autophagy during the acute phase of injury. Although the inflammatory differences were transient, Rubicon mutant mice exhibited improved motor coordination and gait stability during recovery. Proteomic analyses revealed the presence of a truncated Rubicon protein in the mutant mice and identified the negative regulator of reactive oxygen species (NRROS) as a novel interactor of Rubicon. Consistent with this interaction, Rubcn-mutant mice displayed markedly reduced oxidative damage, indicated by decreased lipid peroxidation after injury. Together, these findings indicate that Rubicon promotes acute neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress responses following TBI by modulating autophagy and ROS production. Rubicon-mediated pathways may serve as therapeutic targets to attenuate inflammation-mediated damage after TBI.

title: Base composition reflects RNA polymerase II displacement.
abstract: RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) transcribes all protein-coding and many nonprotein-coding genes in the genome. Pol II transcription termination is crucial for RNA maturation and, when disrupted, can lead to altered RNA processing and RNA export. Termination involves two intertwined processes: RNA cleavage and Pol II release from the DNA (displacement). Despite its importance, the exact mechanisms underlying Pol II displacement from the DNA remain poorly understood. Moreover, under certain cellular stress conditions, there is a partial failure of cleavage, leading to a shift of the position of displacement further downstream, a phenomenon known as readthrough transcription. We present a systematic analysis of Pol II termination across cell types and species and provide novel insights into the mechanism of displacement. Using a probabilistic mixture model to quantify Pol II dynamics across entire gene bodies from nascent RNA sequencing data, we find that genes fall into two classes defined by conserved base composition patterns near the displacement site. Both classes share a T-rich region upstream of displacement, and one class additionally carries a GC-rich region surrounding displacement. We find that GC-rich predisplacement regions have more accessible chromatin and higher levels of phospho-threonine 4 on the CTD of Pol II. Additionally, we find that displacement at genes with only the upstream T-rich pattern are more likely to be affected by perturbations that alter displacement, including heat shock, viral infection, kinase inhibition, and arsenic treatment. Thus, our work identifies two types of Pol II displacement regions, which are differentially affected by perturbations of cellular homeostasis.

title: Suppression of Tau-tubulin kinase 1 mitigates tau phosphorylation, and Aβ mediated neurotoxicity via altered kinase network.
abstract: Tau-tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a neuron-specific serine/threonine tau kinase that is highly expressed in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and phosphorylates microtubule-associated protein tau at sites relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD), thereby contributing to early tau pathology. Targeting TTBK1 can be a promising therapeutic approach for AD, although how suppression of TTBK1 may change neuronal functions is poorly understood. Here we show the proteome and phosphoproteome analysis of murine primary cortical neurons transduced with adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting murine Ttbk1, using tandem mass tag and data independent acquisition liquid chromatography/mass-spectrometry. Suppression of TTBK1 expression by shRNA transduction increases expression of neuronal intermediate filament proteins and V1-domain subunits of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, suggesting the regulatory roles of TTBK1 on cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal activity. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces phosphorylation of TTBK1 and MAP1A as well as increases phosphorylation of neuronal intermediate filament proteins, indicating the regulation of microtubule-related proteins and axonal stabilization. Phosphosite-specific signature analysis identifies the kinases regulated by TTBK1 including AD-related cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and AKT1. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces CDK5 activator p25/p35 ratio and pT231 phospho-tau level, consistent with the reduced activity of CDK5. Finally, silencing of Ttbk1 reduces amyloid-β-induced neurotoxicity in vitro. These results suggest a close functional relationship or coordinated regulation among TTBK1 and other kinases in maintaining axonal homeostasis via phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins, and mediating amyloid-β toxicity, thus emphasize TTBK1 as an emerging therapeutic target of AD.

title: Functional analysis of SmCSN5 in salt stress tolerance of Salvia miltiorrhiza.
abstract: Salt stress limits plant growth, but the contribution of COP9 signalosome subunit 5 (CSN5) to salt tolerance in Salvia miltiorrhiza remains unclear. Here, we combined heterologous overexpression in Arabidopsis thaliana with overexpression and RNA interference in S. miltiorrhiza hairy roots. SmCSN5 transcript abundance increased with NaCl concentration and showed a transient response to 150mM NaCl, peaking at 6h among the sampled times. SmCSN5 overexpression improved germination and growth under salt stress and was associated with higher proline accumulation and antioxidant enzyme activities. Overexpressing Arabidopsis also maintained higher relative water content and chlorophyll content, with lower electrolyte leakage, malondialdehyde content, and ROS-associated staining. Separate ion measurements showed lower Na⁺ content, higher K⁺ content, and lower Na⁺/K⁺ ratios in overexpressing Arabidopsis and hairy roots. SmCSN5 RNA interference produced opposite physiological and ion-accumulation responses in hairy roots. Yeast two-hybrid and luciferase complementation assays identified SmCBL3 as a candidate SmCSN5-interacting protein. Collectively, these findings support a positive role for SmCSN5 in salt tolerance, accompanied by improved antioxidant defense, osmotic adjustment, and ion homeostasis. Whether these responses improve medicinal metabolite production under salinity remains unresolved.

title: VRK1 regulates SRRM2 phosphorylation to promote the splicing of transcripts encoding DNA damage repair factors.
abstract: Vaccinia-related kinase 1 (VRK1) is a nuclear serine/threonine kinase that contributes to genome stability through the phosphorylation of diverse substrates. VRK1 is frequently upregulated in multiple malignancies. Although its function as a chromatin kinase has been extensively characterized, its potential role in RNA processing remains largely unexplored. Using label-free quantitative phosphoproteomics, we identified the splicing scaffold protein serine/arginine repetitive matrix protein 2 (SRRM2) as a high-confidence VRK1-dependent phosphorylation target. We show that VRK1-dependent SRRM2 phosphorylation is required for efficient alternative splicing of DNA damage response (DDR)-related transcripts and contributes to cellular resistance to genotoxic stress. Collectively, this study reveals that VRK1 supports DDR-related splicing by regulating SRRM2 phosphorylation, providing a novel molecular mechanism by which VRK1 contributes to the DNA damage response.

title: RNA polymerase I inhibitor BMH-21 promotes mutant p53 reactivation through nuclear zinc mobilization.
abstract: RNA polymerase I (Pol I) inhibitors activate stress signaling pathways with therapeutic potential in cancer, yet the consequences of Pol I inhibition in p53-mutant tumors remain incompletely understood. Here, we compared the interactions of the Pol I inhibitors CX-5461 and BMH-21 with the p53 reactivators APR-246 and ZMC-1 in p53R175H breast cancer cells. Whereas CX-5461 synergized with p53 reactivators, BMH-21 antagonized these combinations. Unexpectedly, BMH-21 alone restored mutant p53 transcriptional activity and promoted a shift toward a wild-type-like p53 conformation. Mechanistically, BMH-21 increased nuclear labile zinc levels, correlated with degradation of the Pol I catalytic subunit RPA194, and induced stabilization of the zinc-responsive stress factor NRF2. Limiting RPA194 degradation through FBXL14 depletion reduced both nuclear zinc flux and p53-dependent transcriptional activity, supporting a functional link between Pol I destabilization, zinc mobilization, and mutant p53 reactivation. Inhibition of p53 signaling enhanced BMH-21 cytotoxicity, indicating that mutant p53 reactivation promotes a protective stress response rather than cell death. Together, these findings demonstrate that Pol I inhibitors are functionally distinct and identify a previously unrecognized link between Pol I inhibition, zinc homeostasis, and mutant p53 regulation.

title: Delineating plant responses to the 3',5'- and 2',3'-cAMP isomers.
abstract: Much like in animals, both the 3',5'- and the 2,'3'-cAMP isomers are present in plants. The former is the enzymatic product of adenylate cyclases (ACs), the latter is an RNA degradation product. While there is increasing evidence that both isomers can elicit or modulate a broad range of physiological responses, the question of the specificity of responses to isomers has remained, at least partially, unresolved. To delineate isomer-specific responses in Arabidopsis thaliana, we applied a comparative proteomics approach. Our results demonstrate that exposure to 200 nM of either isomer can elicit similar changes in the proteome, supporting the existence of isomer-insensitive targets predominantly involved in RNA processing and metabolism. The 3',5'-specific proteins are enriched in categories such as protein transport and the establishment of protein localization, consistent with the recognised roles of ACs and 3',5'-cAMP in the cytosolic microenvironment. Several RNA-processing components are selectively regulated by the 2',3'-isomer, including proteins that play a critical role in spliceosome stability. At the physiological level, both isomers equally mitigate H2O2-induced net K+ efflux and Ca2+ influx in roots. However, when examining isomer specificity in well-characterized downstream targets, the Cyclic Nucleotide-Gated Channels 2 and 18 (CNGC2 and CNGC18), we noted strict selectivity for 3',5'-cAMP and this would imply that in vivo gating requires catalytically active of ACs.

title: Genetic Biosensors for High-Throughput Biomedical Applications: Challenges and Advances.
abstract: Genetic biosensors represent a particularly promising class of bioengineered instruments designed to enable accurate, real-time monitoring of cellular and molecular processes, with especially strong relevance to high-throughput biomedical workflows. In this review, we provide a systematic, clearly structured overview of the field, covering the fundamental design principles that form the basis of today's platforms. We focus in particular on DNA-based, RNA-based, and CRISPR-based architectures while also examining engineered synthetic biology circuitry, and we place these foundational concepts in the context of more recent advances. These developments encompass improved sensitivity, increased scalability, and broader functionality for multiplexed detection. Beyond summarizing technological progress, we critically evaluate challenges that remain deeply embedded at both technical and biological levels, including limitations driven by signal-to-noise ratio constraints, practical difficulties in delivering probes into cells, and relatively restricted dynamic ranges. Taken together, these issues continue to hinder widespread, routine clinical adoption. Importantly, rather than presenting the topic only as a catalog of improvements, we argue for a unifying framework: the convergence of artificial intelligence and synthetic biology is actively reshaping biosensor engineering, moving it away from a largely empirical, trial-and-error approach toward a more reliable, data-driven discipline. To convert this conceptual shift into tangible outcomes, we also outline a practical implementation framework aimed at reducing the distance between research activities and real-world deployment. This framework emphasizes the need for scalable manufacturing processes, robust and reproducible clinical validation, and regulatory pathways capable of evolving as new evidence emerges. An integrated strategy of this kind is therefore essential for fully realizing the potential of real-time, multichannel biosensing platforms in both complex clinical diagnostics and point-of-care environments.

title: Stage-Associated Efficacy of Systemically Administered Neural Stem Cell-Derived Exosomes in Ischemic Stroke through the Prevention of Cx43 Degradation.
abstract: Ischemic stroke pathology is highly dynamic, making the optimal timing for biological interventions highly elusive. This study investigated the stage-associated therapeutic efficacy of neural stem cell-derived exosomes (NSC-Exos) for cerebral ischemia-reperfusion. The in vivo evaluations identified a restricted therapeutic window closely associated with the temporal evolution of the ischemic microenvironment. Early exosome intervention (4 or 24 h post-ischemia) significantly reduced infarct volume, restored blood-brain barrier integrity, and improved neurological functional recovery. In contrast, delayed administration (48 h) failed to reduce the mortality rate and provide meaningful neuroprotection. To examine the molecular basis of this time dependence, we integrated temporal proteomic profiling of the ischemic penumbra with small RNA sequencing of NSC-Exos. The analytical and functional data suggest that early NSC-Exo delivery transfers miR-9-5p to suppress Nedd4 expression, thereby restoring the Connexin 43 protein pool and stabilizing the astrocytic network to halt initial microenvironmental collapse. Collectively, this study underscores the critical importance of intervention timing and provides a potential translational strategy for utilizing NSC-Exos as a targeted, stage-specific therapy in acute ischemic stroke.

title: Non-adaptive evolutionary forces predominantly shape nucleotide composition near human transcription start sites.
abstract: In the human genome, mutation rates vary along genes, yet how their fine-scale structure contributes to gene evolution has remained largely unexplored. Here, we map inherited mutations at single-nucleotide resolution and uncover a striking hypermutation peak at transcription start sites (TSSs) of human protein-coding genes. This pattern is observed both in population polymorphisms and in de novo mutations from parent-offspring trios, and is dependent on transcriptional activity in testes. We also find similar hypermutation peaks at TSSs used to produce long noncoding RNAs and at intergenic RNA Polymerase II pause sites. In addition, we identify distinct mutational signatures at exon-intron boundaries and in introns. By comparing the current nucleotide content to predicted equilibrium levels, inferred from mutation and fixation rates, and by analyzing derived ancestral frequency spectrums, we detect signals that are compatible with a low level of ongoing background GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) throughout the region and ancestral elevated gBGC activity that is centered right downstream from the TSS. Using a forward-in-time simulation algorithm, we show that the current nucleotide composition surrounding the TSS of protein-coding genes is best explained by local mutation biases coupled to ongoing and ancestral patterns of gene conversions. Our simulations allow us to infer several features of these gBGC events. Overall, these findings indicate that the nucleotide composition around TSSs is largely shaped by non-adaptive forces, particularly mutation bias and gBGC.

title: A Rapid Method to Rank Proteins of Widely Varying Stability: Application to Paramyxovirus Foot Domains.
abstract: The foot domains of polymerases from the Paramyxoviridae family mediate attachment of the viral polymerases to their nucleocapsid templates during viral RNA synthesis. Detailed structural and biophysical characterization of these foot domains reveals that they share a common structure, but when not bound to the nucleocapsid they may exist as intrinsically unstructured chains, molten globules, or highly stable folded domains. With hundreds of paramyxovirus sequences now known, the diverse family of foot domains provides a valuable system to investigate the physical and evolutionary processes that dictate protein stability. To enable rapid and robust evaluation of the relative stability of these domains, we tested the applicability of the split β-lactamase assay. This assay couples β-lactamase activity to the folding of a protein inserted into a loop on the enzyme, with antibiotic resistance being conferred in proportion to the stability of the insert. In this work, five foot domains of broadly varying stability were tested with this assay. We constructed a bespoke vector to facilitate the use of this assay, and we introduced a novel statistical approach that generates a probability-based ranking of relative stability from the experimental data. We find that this assay reproduces the order of stabilities obtained through biophysical approaches. Though classical definitions of stability, evaluated using traditional biophysical techniques, are ill-defined for proteins of low intrinsic stability, this work finds that the split β-lactamase assay can be fruitfully adapted in such cases, and can be made more convenient and interpreted more rigorously through the innovations we describe. © 2026 The Author(s). title: Endogenous Protein Tagging in Postmitotic Neurons via Lentiviral and Adeno-associated Virus Delivery.
abstract: This protocol describes a method for endogenous protein tagging in postmitotic primary neurons using homology-independent targeted integration (HITI), a CRISPR/Cas9-based approach that exploits non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Unlike homology-directed repair (HDR), HITI does not require cell division, making it uniquely suited for postmitotic neurons. SpCas9 is delivered by a replication-incompetent simian immunodeficiency lentiviral vector (pLenti SIV), while the sgRNA, donor tag cassette, and a fluorescent plasma membrane marker are co-packaged in a single AAV vector. The two vectors are co-delivered at DIV5, and endogenous tagging is assessed at DIV15-23. The workflow is illustrated using Junctophilin-3 (JPH3) tagged with mEmerald at its endogenous locus. Airyscan microscopy imaging of endogenously tagged JPH3 at native expression levels revealed its localization at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane (ER-PM) contact sites and uncovered a periodic distribution of ER-PM junctions along the dendritic arbor, enabling identification of a previously unrecognized ladder-like organization of the ER in neuronal dendrites. Genomic integration of the tag is validated at both 5' and 3' junctions by next-generation sequencing. The protocol can be adapted to other neuronal proteins by redesigning the guide RNA and donor sequence, and supports fluorescent proteins as well as epitope and self-labeling tags. The plasma membrane marker can also be replaced with other fluorescent reporters or markers for intracellular organelles to assess infection efficiency and verify subcellular localization of the protein of interest. The full workflow takes 5-6 weeks. © 2026 The Author(s). Current Protocols published by Wiley Periodicals LLC. Protocols included in this article: Basic Protocol 1: sgRNA design and HITI donor vector cloning Basic Protocol 2: Primary rat neuron culture and viral co-transduction Basic Protocol 3: Live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged proteins Support Protocol 1: Production of lentiviral and AAV particles Support Protocol 2: Validation of knock-in by next-generation sequencing (NGS).

title: Nanotechnology-Driven Precision Diagnostics and Therapeutics for Preeclampsia.
abstract: Preeclampsia originates in placental dysfunction yet it is detected only after maternal hypertension and proteinuria or other organ damage emerge, by which point disease-modifying interventions are not available, and delivery of the baby and placenta remains the only cure. Nanotechnology offers a route to reduce this diagnostic-therapeutic latency. Nanostructured biosensors and liquid biopsy platforms detect placental proteins, cell-free RNA/DNA, and extracellular vesicles at femtomolar concentrations and in a multiplex manner, enabling earlier risk stratification when integrated with machine-learning models. In parallel, placenta-targeted lipid-, peptide-, polymeric-, dendrimeric-, and small extracellular vesicle-based nanocarriers deliver angiogenic mRNA, antiangiogenic siRNA, antioxidants, and immunomodulators selectively to the trophoblast cells while limiting fetal exposure. Placenta-on-a-chip platforms and ex vivo placental perfusion models provide human-relevant test beds for these systems. We critically appraise these advances, examine the safety-by-design, manufacturing bottlenecks, and regulatory constraints unique to obstetric nanomedicine, and outline the convergence of theranostics and digital health that could move preeclampsia care from reactive symptom management toward proactive, placenta-targeted monitoring and therapy.

title: m7G modification in mRNA cooperates with QKI to promote homologous recombination repair.
abstract: DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired through distinct pathways, with homologous recombination (HR) favored when DNA ends undergo extensive resection. Although cytoplasmic N7-methylguanosine (m7G)-modified RNA increases after UV-induced single-strand breaks, its role in DSB repair (including HR) remains unclear. Here, we show that m7G-modified RNA accumulates at DSB sites, where it recruits the m7G reader protein Quaking (QKI)5, to selectively promote HR. Mechanistically, QKI5 directly interacts with MRE11 and enhances its DNA binding affinity, thereby facilitating DNA end resection. Depletion of QKI5 impairs recruitment of the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 complex to DSBs and reduces HR repair efficiency. Moreover, elevated QKI5 expression is associated with resistance to radiotherapy in both mouse models and clinical cohorts. Together, these findings identify the m7G RNA-QKI5-MRE11 axis as a regulator of HR pathway choice and suggest QKI5 as a promising therapeutic target in cancer treatment.
extra: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

title: Cas13d-Mediated Knockdown of Long Noncoding RNAs.
abstract: CRISPR-Cas13 systems represent a powerful and programmable platform for RNA-targeted applications, including RNA knockdown. Long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), which lacks an open reading frame and is thereby often refractory to Cas9-mediated indel production, can be successfully knocked down by Cas13 systems. DeepCas13, a deep learning-based model, was developed to predict Cas13d on-target activity for RNA interference with high accuracy. Here, we describe detailed protocols about sgRNA design and experimental procedures for the lentiviral vector-based CRISPR-Cas13 system to knock down individual lncRNAs. Our protocol can be naturally extended to knockdown other types of coding and noncoding RNAs, including messenger RNA (mRNA) circular RNA (circRNA).

title: Interleukin-35 Ameliorates Obesity-Associated Impairment of Endothelium-Dependent Vasodilation via the STAT3-MAPK/ERK-eNOS Signaling Axis.
abstract: Obesity impairs endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS)-nitric oxide (NO) signaling, triggering chronic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction and defective vasodilation, which drives cardiometabolic diseases. Existing metabolic therapies provide only indirect vascular protection and fail to resolve residual inflammatory-mediated cardiovascular risk. As an anti-inflammatory interleukin 12 (IL-12) family cytokine, interleukin 35 (IL-35) is suppressed in obesity and exerts vascular protective effects under inflammatory conditions, yet its function and underlying mechanisms in obesity‑related endothelial vasodilator dysfunction remain undefined. An obese mouse model was established by 8-week high-fat diet (HFD) feeding, followed by 4-week intraperitoneal administration of recombinant mouse IL-35. Aortic-ring assays evaluated vasodilatory function. Palmitic acid (PA)-treated human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), recapitulate lipotoxic endothelial injury, were treated with recombinant human IL-35. Western blotting, immunofluorescence, 4-amino-5-methylamino-2',7'-difluorofluorescein diacetate (DAF-FM DA) detection and immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) were applied to detect IL-35-subunit (Epstein-Barr virus-induced gene 3 [EBI3] and interleukin-12 subunit alpha [IL-12A]) levels, eNOS Ser1177 phosphorylation, phosphorylation of mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (MAPK/ERK) signaling molecules (cellular rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma [cRAF], mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase [MEK], and ERK) and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) activation, NO production, and eNOS-binding partners. Rescue assays were performed using Raf or ERK specific inhibitors and STAT3 small interfering RNA (siRNA). HFD mice displayed reduced aortic endothelial EBI3 expression, impaired endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation, decreased eNOS Ser1177 phosphorylation and lowered NO production; all these phenotypes were rescued by exogenous IL-35. IP-MS and immunoblotting demonstrated that IL-35 strengthened eNOS-ERK1 interaction and restored PA-repressed phosphorylation of cRAF, MEK, ERK and eNOS Ser1177, which were abrogated by Raf or ERK blockade. Furthermore, IL-35 recovered STAT3 phosphorylation suppressed by PA, while STAT3 knockdown blunted IL-35-driven MAPK/ERK activation, eNOS phosphorylation and subsequent NO production. IL-35 alleviates obesity-induced impairment of endothelium-dependent vasodilation via the STAT3-MAPK/ERK-eNOS axis, which elevates eNOS Ser1177 phosphorylation and NO synthesis. This work supports IL-35 as a prospective therapeutic candidate for obesity-associated vascular complications.

title: PDGF-BB secreted by OTSCC orchestrates CAF-driven tumor progression through regulating the LINC00886/hsa-miR-15b-5p/AKT axis.
abstract: Under the induction of factors derived from tumor cells, fibroblasts can transform into cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), in which non-coding RNAs play a key role. This study aims to reveal the regulatory mechanisms of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in CAFs induced by PDGF-BB from oral tongue squamous carcinoma cells. This study found that PDGF-BB effectively induces the transformation of fibroblasts into cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). Through focused analysis of transcriptional results, it was discovered that LINC00886 is significantly overexpressed in CAFs (PDGF-BB). Furthermore, knocking down LINC00886 in CAFs (PDGF-BB) resulted in a reversal of related CAF markers, including downregulation of CAF marker proteins, reduced lactate secretion, and inhibition of aerobic glycolysis. Additionally, as a long non-coding RNA, LINC00886 regulates cellular biological behaviors through interactions with miRNAs. Predictions from the ENCORI online database revealed that LINC00886 can interact with hsa-miR-15b-5p. Further analysis indicated that the AKT-mTOR signaling pathway is inhibited in the transcriptome data of CAFs with knocked-down LINC00886. When an inhibitor of hsa-miR-15b-5p was added to CAFs (sh-LINC00886), the total AKT protein level was significantly upregulated, and the phosphorylation level of mTOR was also upregulated. This result was confirmed in a xenograft model. Our study demonstrates that PDGF-BB induces the transformation of fibroblasts into CAFs and thereby promotes tumor progression by regulating the LINC00886/hsa-miR-15b-5p/AKT signaling axis, providing new potential targets for cancer therapy.

title: A trifluoromethylated chalcone derivative attenuates Alzheimer disease-related Aβ/Tau pathology by modulating the AMPK-dependent autophagy-proteostasis axis.
abstract: Impaired autophagic clearance contributes to proteostasis failure and the accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) and pathological Tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet pharmacologically tractable activators of productive autophagy remain limited. Here, we screened an in-house library of 64 natural products, semisynthetic derivatives, and synthetic analogues and identified compound 51 (C51), a synthetic trifluoromethylated 4-hydroxy-3-methoxy chalcone derivative, as an activator of autophagy. C51 enhanced autophagic flux, lysosomal activity, and SQSTM1/p62 turnover in mammalian cells and Caenorhabditis elegans, indicating productive autophagic clearance rather than autophagosome accumulation. C51 reduced APP-, Tau-, and TauP301L-associated proteotoxicity in neuronal cells and ameliorated Aβ- and Tau-related behavioral deficits, protein aggregation, Tau phosphorylation, and oxidative stress in transgenic C. elegans. In 3×Tg-AD mice, C51 improved learning and memory, preserved hippocampal neurons and synaptic proteins, and reduced gliosis, Aβ oligomer accumulation, and phosphorylated Tau burden without overt systemic toxicity. Mechanistically, C51 activated AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and suppressed mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, together with drug affinity-responsive target stability and cellular thermal shift assays, supported C51-AMPK interaction. AMPK knockdown, Compound C, and aak-2 RNA interference markedly attenuated C51-induced autophagy and protection against Aβ/Tau toxicity, demonstrating a conserved requirement for AMPK signaling. Quantitative proteomics further showed that C51 rebalanced TauP301L-disrupted proteostasis networks. Collectively, C51 represents a potent natural product-inspired autophagy activator with therapeutic potential for AD by restoring AMPK-dependent autophagic clearance and Aβ/Tau proteostasis across complementary AD models.

title: Functional Characterization of a Novel FADD from Anodonta woodiana Reveals Its Regulatory Roles in Apoptotic Cascades and Antibacterial Immunity.
abstract: Fas-associated death domain (FADD) is a core conserved adaptor in death receptor-induced apoptotic signaling pathway that plays a crucial role in apoptosis and innate immunity in vertebrates. However, the function of FADDs in invertebrates, especially in bivalve mollusks, remains elusive. In the present study, a novel molluscan FADD homolog (AwFADD) was identified and functionally characterized from the bivalve Anodonta woodiana. The AwFADD protein consists of 232 amino acids and harbors two conserved functional domains: an N-terminal death effector domain (DED) and a C-terminal death domain (DD). Tissue expression profiling revealed that AwFADD was ubiquitously expressed in all examined tissues, with predominant expression in the hepatopancreas and hemocytes. Upon challenge with Aeromonas hydrophila or lipopolysaccharide, AwFADD mRNA expression was upregulated in hemocytes of A. woodiana, implying its potential involvement in host antibacterial responses. RNA interference‑mediated knockdown of AwFADD suppressed the expression of AwCaspase-8/-3, whereas it enhanced transcripts of MyD88-dependent pathway genes and downstream immune-related effectors in hemocytes in response to A. hydrophila infection. Subcellular localization analysis suggested that AwFADD was predominantly localized in the cytoplasm of HEK293T cells. Dual-luciferase reporter assays further indicated that AwFADD overexpression enhanced the activation of NF-κB and AP-1 in a dose-dependent manner under basal conditions, but suppressed MyD88-triggered NF-κB/AP-1 signaling activation. These findings suggest that AwFADD may serve as a crucial bifunctional regulator that integrates apoptotic cascade activation and MyD88-dependent antibacterial immune responses in A. woodiana.

title: Transcriptomics of independent CRISPR-edited cell lines reveal ciliary-specific ARL13B dependent changes.
abstract: Primary cilia coordinate signaling pathways that regulate tissue homeostasis and development, and defects in cilia contribute to numerous ciliopathies. However, the transcriptional consequences of disrupting ciliary protein localization remain poorly defined. ARL13B is a cilia-enriched regulatory GTPase required for ciliary trafficking and signaling. The ARL13BV358A variant is undetectable in cilia yet retains known biochemical functions, providing a unique model to investigate the functions of ciliary ARL13B independently of ciliogenesis. To define transcriptional programs associated with loss of ciliary ARL13B, we generated two independent Arl13bV358A/V358A kidney epithelial cell lines and matched rescue lines. The ARL13BV358A mutation did not affect ciliation frequency or cilia length but altered ciliary protein composition, including loss of ARL3 and INPP5E localization and increased accumulation of TULP3. RNA sequencing revealed expression changes in genes associated with ciliary biology, mechanotransduction, epithelial organization, and kidney-related phenotypes. Despite similar ciliary phenotypes, the independently-derived, mutant clones displayed substantial transcriptomic heterogeneity, highlighting a potential source of variation in CRISPR-based transcriptional studies. By integrating data from the independent mutant and rescue clones, we identified a high-confidence set of 131 genes whose expression reproducibly tracked with loss and restoration of ciliary ARL13B. Together, these findings demonstrate that ciliary ARL13B is required to maintain normal ciliary composition and gene expression programs and underscores the value of multi-clone, rescue-based experimental designs for robust transcriptomic analyses.

title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer.
abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

title: The role of 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase (OAS) proteins in HIV infection: innate antiviral immunity, viral persistence, and therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) establishes persistent infection despite robust innate immune responses and effective antiretroviral therapy, highlighting the importance of host antiviral mechanisms in regulating viral replication and persistence. Among interferon-stimulated genes, 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase 1 (OAS1) is a key antiviral effector that senses viral double-stranded RNA and activates the OAS-RNase L pathway. Beyond its canonical antiviral activity, emerging evidence implicates OAS1 in immune regulation, viral latency, neuroinflammation, and retroviral disease progression. This review examines the genomic organization, structural diversity, isoform-specific functions, genetic variation, and interferon-mediated regulation of the OAS protein family, emphasizing OAS1 in HIV infection. Experimental and clinical studies indicate that type I and type III interferons induce OAS1 in macrophages, dendritic cells, epithelial and endothelial cells, microglia, and lymphocytes, contributing to HIV restriction through RNase L activation and enhanced innate antiviral responses. OAS signalling may also support mucosal antiviral defence, regulate viral burden and chronic immune activation, influence interferon responsiveness during combination antiretroviral therapy, and contribute to central nervous system protection. Conversely, dysregulated OAS1 expression has been associated with HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders. Genetic polymorphisms and alternative splicing generate functional diversity in OAS1, potentially influencing antiviral activity, individual susceptibility, and clinical outcomes. Collectively, available evidence positions OAS1 as a multifunctional antiviral and immunoregulatory component of host defence that may influence multiple aspects of HIV pathogenesis. Further investigation into OAS1 activation, genetic variation, isoform-specific functions, and immune modulation may facilitate biomarker discovery and support the development of host-directed therapeutic strategies against persistent retroviral infections.

title: UPF1-mediated mRNA decay promotes melanoma tumorigenesis through miR-101-3p-dependent destabilization of NANOS1.
abstract: Numerous studies have reported Up-frameshift protein 1 (UPF1) as a crucial posttranscriptional regulator in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), attributing its role to tumorigenesis across various cancers. However, its recently unveiled function in UPF1-mediated mRNA decay (UMD), intricately coordinated with miRNA, remains unexplored in the context of tumorigenesis. Here, we demonstrate that UPF1 contributes to melanoma tumorigenesis by regulating NANOS1 expression in a miR-101-3p-dependent manner. Depletion of UPF1 across three melanoma cell lines significantly impaired cell growth, migration, and invasion by cell cycle arrest and disrupted tumor formation in vivo. Through comprehensive RNA-seq and biochemical analyses, we elucidate that attenuation of UPF1 leads to an increase in NANOS1 expression, consequently suppressing melanoma tumorigenesis. Mechanistically, UPF1 orchestrates the destabilization of NANOS1 via UPF1-mediated mRNA decay (UMD) facilitated by miR-101-3p. Intriguingly, UPF1 depletion and NANOS1 upregulation were associated with reduced ERK and ELK1 phosphorylation, suggesting that attenuation of MAPK/ERK/ELK1 signaling may contribute, at least in part, to the observed melanoma-suppressive phenotypes. Importantly, the biological relevance of UPF1 and NANOS1 in melanoma cell lines was further supported in drug-resistant melanoma cells and in xenograft mouse models. Collectively, these findings expand our understanding of UMD in melanoma and identify the UPF1/NANOS1 regulatory relationship as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in both parental and drug-resistant melanoma cells.

title: Targeting lactate-driven protein lactylation overcomes proteasome inhibitor resistance in multiple myeloma.
abstract: Acquired resistance to proteasome inhibitors (PIs) remains a major challenge limiting the long-term efficacy of multiple myeloma (MM) therapy, while the metabolic-epigenetic mechanisms underlying PI resistance remain incompletely defined. Using clinical bone marrow specimens, paired parental and PI-resistant MM cell models, xenografts, and integrated lactylome, CUT&Tag, and RNA-seq profiling, we investigated the role of lactate-associated lactylation in acquired PI resistance. Bone marrow lactate levels, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) activity, and global protein lactylation were elevated in relapsed/refractory MM and in PI-resistant cell models. Lactylome profiling revealed extensive lactylation remodeling and identified histone H4K12 lactylation (H4K12la) as a prominent resistance-associated epigenetic mark. Integrative prioritization and functional validation identified EP300 as an upstream regulator of H4K12la; EP300 was upregulated in resistant cells, and its depletion reduced H4K12la and partially restored PI sensitivity. Integration of H4K12la CUT&Tag and RNA-seq linked resistance-associated H4K12la remodeling to autophagy/lysosome-related transcriptional programs, with increased H4K12la occupancy at the Cathepsin L (CTSL) promoter accompanied by increased CTSL expression. Pharmacological LDH inhibition with FX-11 reduced H4K12la and CTSL expression. Moreover, combining FX-11 with carfilzomib markedly enhanced antitumor activity in a PI-resistant MM xenograft model without detectable systemic or hematological toxicity during the treatment period. Collectively, these findings define a lactate-EP300-H4K12la-CTSL pathway that contributes to PI resistance and provide a preclinical rationale for combined metabolic and proteasomal inhibition in refractory MM.

title: Ketamine Beyond Anaesthesia: Analgesic, Psychiatric, Antitumour, and Immunomodulatory Actions and Their Signalling Mechanisms.
abstract: To synthesize current evidence on ketamine for cancer-related pain and its intersecting psychiatric, anti-tumor, and immunomodulatory actions, emphasizing mechanisms, clinical relevance, and uncertainties relevant to oncology. Ketamine provides analgesia primarily through non-competitive antagonism of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors and additional effects on excitatory, inhibitory, and opioid-related signaling. In patients with refractory cancer pain, it may be a useful adjunct to opioid-based multimodal analgesia and may reduce opioid requirements; however, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Its rapid antidepressant effects may be relevant to the reciprocal burden of pain and depressive symptoms in cancer. Preclinical studies report antiproliferative, pro-apoptotic, and ferroptosis-associated effects across several tumor models, involving phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mechanistic target of rapamycin, extracellular signal-regulated kinase, and non-coding RNA-associated pathways. These findings are not uniform: breast cancer models have suggested potentially pro-metastatic effects. Immune effects are likewise dose-, context-, and perioperative-setting dependent, with reports of anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive, and neutral effects. Ketamine is a potentially valuable opioid-sparing adjunct for selected patients with cancer-related pain and may also address comorbid depressive symptoms. Its putative direct anti-tumor and immunomodulatory actions remain predominantly preclinical and context dependent and should not currently guide oncologic treatment decisions. Appropriately powered clinical studies should define patient selection, dose and route, duration, safety, immune consequences, and long-term oncologic outcomes.

title: Luteolin protects against cholestasis by suppressing hepatocyte apoptosis through direct PI3K binding and AKT activation.
abstract: Excessive hepatocyte apoptosis triggered by toxic bile acids is the core pathological event of cholestasis, and the direct target of luteolin (Lut), the major bioactive constituent of Siphonostegia chinensis Benth., for this protective effect remains unclear. This study aims to elucidate how Lut suppresses hepatocyte apoptosis and ameliorates cholestatic liver injury. A murine cholestasis model was induced by α-naphthylisothiocyanate (ANIT), and the hepatocyte apoptotic pathways were validated in glycochenodeoxycholic acid (GCDCA)-treated HepG2 cells. Liver tissue pathological changes were assessed via hematoxylin-eosin (HE) histological staining. Network pharmacology paired with supplementary RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was used to screen candidate pathways contributing to Lut's anti-cholestatic effects. Quantitative real-time PCR, Western blotting and Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) immunostaining were jointly utilized to assess apoptotic levels in liver parenchymal cells. Additionally, surface plasmon resonance (SPR) coupled with molecular docking simulations was adopted to clarify the direct binding profile of Lut. Lut treatment markedly ameliorated serum biochemical indices and liver histopathological lesions in ANIT-exposed mice. Meanwhile, oxidative stress was alleviated, bile acid transporters were restored, inflammatory cytokines declined, and hepatocyte apoptosis was suppressed. Network pharmacology combined with RNA-seq predicted that Lut alleviates cholestasis through the Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Protein Kinase B (PI3K/AKT)-mediated anti-apoptotic pathway. This hypothesis was further supported by TUNEL, Western blotting, and qRT-PCR analyses, which indicated that Lut could activate the PI3K/AKT, and then suppress hepatocyte apoptosis in cholestasis. SPR analysis revealed a concentration-dependent direct interaction between Lut and PI3K with a kinetic KD of 9.036 × 10-5 M, and molecular docking revealed a plausible binding mode within the kinase domain. Additionally, the anti-apoptotic effect of Lut was largely abolished when PI3K was inhibited by LY294002 in vitro. This study is the first to confirm that Lut directly targets PI3K to initiate the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade, and thereby suppresses bile acid-induced hepatocyte apoptosis. These findings refine the mechanistic understanding of Lut's hepatoprotective action from general antioxidant activity to target-specific anti-apoptotic signaling, and provide a molecular explanation for the traditional use of S. chinensis Benth. for the treatment of damp-heat jaundice.

title: Liver-resident cellular determinants of oncolytic virotherapy in hepatocellular carcinoma: viral susceptibility and spatial immune remodeling.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) develops in a chronically injured and immunologically specialized organ that is both the treatment target and a major determinant of viral clearance and toxicity. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) can couple tumor-selective infection with immunogenic lysis, innate sensing, antigen presentation, and adaptive immune recruitment, but the clinical consequences of these processes depend on viral platform, delivery route, liver-resident cell handling, spatial disease distribution, and hepatic reserve. This review synthesizes HCC OV biology across four linked levels: platform-specific tumor-cell susceptibility; replication and interferon restriction; regulation by Kupffer cells, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, dendritic-cell subsets, hepatic stellate cells, fibroblasts, and resident lymphoid populations; and spatial pharmacodynamics across injected tumors, non-injected intrahepatic lesions, cirrhotic parenchyma, and extrahepatic disease. We compare adenovirus, vaccinia virus, herpes simplex virus, and candidate RNA viruses using route- and assay-matched criteria and interpret clinical evidence according to study design, biological context, and permissible inference. Early Pexa-Vec studies established biological activity, whereas PHOCUS defined a negative boundary for Pexa-Vec followed by sorafenib in an unselected first-line population. H101 plus nivolumab and VG161 support early feasibility and pharmacodynamic investigation, while integrated human pharmacodynamic and diseased-liver HCC-model reovirus data highlight schedule-dependent immune effects and potential off-tumor liver inflammation. VIRAL-HCC is used only as a non-scored organizational matrix for prospective trial design and biomarker interpretation. Future development should link tumor exposure and productive infection or payload expression to compartment-resolved immune effects, clinically relevant tumor control, and preservation of hepatic reserve.

title: Inter-individual gene expression variability implies stable regulation of brain-biased genes across organs in three ray-finned fishes.
abstract: Phenotypic variation among individuals provides the raw material for evolution, and gene expression is a key mediator between genetic and phenotypic variation. As for phenotypes, the range of gene expression is limited and biased by evolutionary and developmental constraints. Observed expression variability due to biomolecular stochasticity and cell-to-cell heterogeneity has been well-studied in isogenic populations of unicellular organisms. However, for multicellular organisms with a diversity of cells and tissues sharing the same genetic background, the interplay between expression variability, gene and organ function, and gene regulation remains an open question. Here, we use highly multiplexed 3'-end bulk RNA sequencing to generate transcriptome profiles spanning at least nine organs in outbred individuals of three ray-finned fish species: zebrafish, Northern pike, and spotted gar. Per organ, we quantify individual-to-individual gene expression variability independent of mean expression level. Lowly variable genes are enriched in cellular housekeeping functions whereas highly variable genes are enriched in stimulus-response functions. Furthermore, highly variable genes evolve under weaker purifying selection at the protein-coding sequence, indicating that intra-species expression variability predicts inter-species protein sequence divergence. Genes that are broadly expressed across organs are both highly expressed and lowly variable, whereas organ-biased genes are typically highly variable within their top organ. Among organ-biased genes, patterns of expression variance are dependent on the top organ. Specifically, brain- and gonads-biased genes have lowly variable expression across different organs, suggesting stabilizing selection. These patterns suggest that gene regulatory mechanisms evolve under organ-specific selective pressures.

title: Deep Intact Glycoproteomic Analysis Reveals Multi-Level Glycosylation Heterogeneity in Renal Tumors.
abstract: Extensive changes in glycosylation are observed in many malignancies, but limited information is available about the modified proteins and sites. We used intact glycoproteomics to map N-glycosites in 32 surgically resected renal tumors and paired adjacent normal tissues. We identified 853,340 total and 54,354 unique N-linked glycopeptides from 1,940 glycoproteins containing 220 glycan compositions. The Shannon diversity index was used to characterize glycosylation diversity and identified tumor-associated differences enriched in glycoproteins mapping to cell-adhesion and immunity processes. Although more glycopeptides were identified in tumors, whole-glycoproteome Shannon diversity did not differ significantly between tissue types; tumor-associated differences were concentrated at specific glycoproteins and glycosites. . In tumors, complex fucosylated and complex sialylated glycans were more common. RNA-seq and uniLASSO-based integration nominated glycosylation-related transcripts associated with site-specific glycan-category changes. Changes in total protein abundance were moderately associated with changes in Shannon diversity at the protein (R2 = 0.290) and glycosite (R2 = 0.279) levels, but most of the linear variation was not accounted for by protein abundance alone. Diversity changes were also concentrated in functional and structural protein domains. The results provide prioritized candidates and hypotheses for independent validation and mechanistic studies of protein glycosylation changes in renal tumors.

title: Single-nucleotide polymorphism-directed design of allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3.
abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also called Machado-Joseph disease, the most common form of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3. The mutant protein is prone to aggregation and exerts toxic gain-of-function effects, whereas the wild-type protein has important neuroprotective roles as a deubiquitinase. Current treatment strategies for SCA3 lack specificity for the mutant allele. Identifying genetic variants such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in linkage with the pathogenic CAG expansion offers a promising avenue to develop allele-specific therapeutic interventions, like antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). To address this, we conducted allele-specific, targeted, multiplexed nanopore sequencing on 79 patients with SCA3 from Germany, UK, and Portugal. We identified almost 200 polymorphisms and grouped them into three haplotype blocks on the basis of linkage disequilibrium. These SNPs were strongly associated with the CAG expansion. Genotypic modeling of our subcohorts indicated that targeting only two SNPs from different blocks could enable allele-specific treatment of the majority of European patients with SCA3. We evaluated 17 candidate ASOs targeting SNPs from different haplotype blocks. Seven of these ASOs caused allele-preferential reduction of more than 65%. A single ASO application in two SCA3 iPSC-derived cortical neurons (AX1, AX2) achieved up to 90% reduction of mutant ATXN3. Toxicity assessments together with RNA sequencing analyses in AX1 did not indicate evidence of toxicity or widespread transcriptional perturbations. These findings highlight that characterizing heterozygosity rates offers valuable opportunities for selective ASO therapies. Our proof-of-principle targeting with ASOs demonstrates the feasibility of haplotype-informed allele-specific silencing in ATXN3.

title: Grapevine rust fungus Neophysopella tropicalis deploys protein effectors with plant immunity-suppressing activity during sequential stages of pathogenesis.
abstract: Germination of urediniospores marks the onset of infection by Neophysopella tropicalis, the causal agent of Asian grapevine leaf rust, yet the molecular mechanisms enabling this obligate biotrophic fungus to establish infection remain largely unknown. We combined transcriptomics, histological analyses, and functional assays to identify and characterize candidate effector proteins deployed during the earliest stages of pathogenesis. RNA sequencing of in vitro-germinated urediniospores identified 303 genes encoding predicted secreted proteins bearing hallmarks of fungal effectors, grouped into 142 sequence families and revealing a remarkably diverse repertoire of effector candidates. Fifteen highly expressed N. tropicalis effector candidate (NtEC) genes, representing thirteen distinct sequence families, were selected for expression profiling by reverse transcription quantitative PCR across infection stages. Chitin-targeted fluorescence microscopy provided a developmental framework for interpreting expression across germination, penetration, and early colonization. Although identified during germination, seven NtECs accumulated transcripts predominantly during host penetration and early biotrophic colonization, suggesting specialized roles in infection establishment. Using the Type III Secretion System of Pseudomonas fluorescens EtHAn, we demonstrated that three NtECs (NtEC-05, NtEC-09, and NtEC-10) strongly suppressed AvrB-triggered hypersensitive cell death in Nicotiana benthamiana, while three others (NtEC-11, NtEC-12, and NtEC-13) exhibited moderate immune-suppressing activity. Together, these findings provide the first comprehensive characterization of the N. tropicalis effector repertoire, demonstrating that early infection involves coordinated, sequential deployment of evolutionarily diverse effectors associated with plant immune suppression. This work establishes an integrated framework for discovery and functional prioritization of rust fungus effectors and provides a valuable molecular resource for future studies on grapevine-rust interactions.

title: Multivariate Genome-Wide Analysis Delineates Shared Genetic Determinants Across Periodontal and Oral Microbial Phenotypes.
abstract: Periodontitis affects approximately 10% of the global population, posing a serious threat to tooth retention and quality of life. The disease emerges from bidirectional host-microbiome interactions that can shift from homeostasis to dysbiosis and chronic inflammation, yet conventional single-phenotype analyses cannot resolve pleiotropic loci acting across interrelated periodontal and microbial traits. We aimed to jointly model the shared genetic structure of six periodontitis-related phenotypes and to prioritise pleiotropic loci with translational relevance. We harmonised European-ancestry genome-wide association studies (GWAS) summary statistics for six traits representing host periodontal phenotypes (gingivitis, chronic periodontitis, periapical abscess, dental calculus) and oral microbial composition (genus Porphyromonas, order Bacteroidales). A common genetic factor was estimated using genomic structural equation modelling (genomic SEM), and factor-level genome-wide association analysis was conducted on 4,899,781 SNPs. The resulting signals were annotated through locus discovery and novelty assessment (FUMA), fine-mapping (SuSiE and FINEMAP), gene-level testing (MAGMA), and transcriptome-wide association with Bayesian gene prioritisation (FUSION and FOCUS). Heritability was partitioned across functional annotations (stratified LD score regression), and cell types (CELLECT); spatial enrichment was assessed using gsMap, and a polygenic risk score was constructed with PRS-CS. A single-factor model provided adequate fit (CFI = 1.0). Factor-level GWAS identified 127 genome-wide significant SNPs consolidating into 56 independent lead variants, all uniquely identified at the factor level. MAGMA prioritised RASAL2 and C5orf27. Fine-mapping yielded 56 variants with posterior inclusion probabilities exceeding 0.95. Transcriptome-wide association and FOCUS converged on the long non-coding RNA RP11-563N4.1 (PIP = 1). Cell-type enrichment highlighted a vascular-stromal axis led by hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, with additional signals in pericytes, cardiac and smooth muscle cells, endocardium, and lung stroma. Spatial mapping localised the strongest aggregate signal to lung tissue, consistent with an oral-lung mucosal axis. Polygenic risk was distributed unevenly across chromosomes. These analyses delineate a vascular-matrix-centred genetic architecture shared across periodontal and oral microbial traits. The prioritised loci and effector genes provide genetically informed candidates for risk stratification and for targeted investigation of periodontal pathobiology. Clinically, these genetically informed candidates may aid in identifying individuals at elevated risk and in guiding mechanism-based preventive and therapeutic strategies for periodontitis.

title: Discovery and optimization of N-phenylbenzenesulfonamide analogues as novel ALKBH5 inhibitors for AML therapy.
abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive malignancy with poor prognosis, primarily driven by leukemic stem cells (LSCs). The RNA demethylase ALKBH5 is aberrantly overexpressed in AML and critically involved in leukemogenesis and LSC maintenance. Herein, we designed and synthesized fifty-seven N-phenylbenzenesulfonamide derivatives as potential ALKBH5 inhibitors. Within this series, G4 emerged as a potent ALKBH5 inhibitor that selectively suppressed ALKBH5-high AML cells over ALKBH5-knockout cells and normal human PBMCs. In G4-treated AML cells, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis were accompanied by dose-dependent reductions in MCL-1 and Bcl-xL protein levels. Genetic knockout of ALKBH5 markedly attenuated G4-induced cytotoxicity, supporting the ALKBH5 dependence of G4 activity. CETSA and SPR further supported a direct interaction between G4 and ALKBH5. MD simulations and 2-OG competition assays suggested the involvement of the 2-OG pocket in G4 recognition. Mechanistically, G4 directly inhibited ALKBH5 and elevated global m6A levels. Consistently, G4 dose-dependently downregulated TACC3, a known ALKBH5 target, impaired LSC self-renewal, and showed significant in vivo anti-AML efficacy. Collectively, these findings identify G4 as an ALKBH5 inhibitor that impairs LSCs self-renewal with robust in vivo efficacy, providing a promising lead for further optimization toward AML therapy.

title: Untranslated Region-FNex: An Integrative Multimodal Framework for Functional Untranslated Region Variant Prioritization.
abstract: Genetic variants in untranslated regions (UTRs) can alter post-transcriptional regulation, yet functional interpretation remains difficult because regulatory mechanisms differ between 5'UTR and 3'UTR contexts and are not fully captured by generic noncoding-variant scores. We developed UTR-FNex, an interpretable machine-learning framework for prioritizing candidate functional variants in both UTR regions. We first constructed MetaUTR, a harmonized resource of approximately 200,000 UTR variant loci, and derived model-development sets containing 14,627 3'UTR and 3533 5'UTR variants after confidence-based filtering. UTR-FNex integrates region-specific sequence, RNA-structure, regulatory-motif, miRNA, conservation, and DNABERT-derived allele representations, with a neural feature enhancement (NFE) module providing additional interaction summaries. Across 10 repeated random hold-outs, mean AUROCs were 0.876 for 3'UTR and 0.974 for 5'UTR. Under gene-grouped evaluation, AUROCs decreased to 0.769 and 0.672, respectively, indicating substantial context dependence, especially for 5'UTR. In an external prostate-cancer 3'UTR cohort, UTR-FNex achieved an AUROC of 0.720 (95% CI 0.690-0.750), compared with 0.696 (95% CI 0.660-0.733) for FunUV; however, FunUV achieved higher AUPRC and stronger top-k enrichment. A TP53 rs78378222 case study connected model sensitivity to a known polyadenylation-signal context, whereas RNAfold-derived differences were window-dependent and were treated as exploratory. These results support UTR-FNex as a multimodal prioritization framework while defining important limits in cross-gene and cross-source generalization. Source code is available at https://github.com/liyaning233/UTR-FNex, and MetaUTR is deposited at 10.5281/zenodo.19719670.

title: Lentiviral RNAi for Depletion of Enhancer RNAs in Primary Neurons.
abstract: Enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) are non-polyadenylated long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) transcribed from active enhancer regions and are increasingly recognized as key regulators of cell-type-specific gene expression. Noncoding RNAs exist in multiple forms and contribute to both transcriptional and posttranscriptional processes. Understanding their biological functions often requires selective depletion of individual RNA molecules. However, unlike protein-coding transcripts, eRNAs lack stable 3' ends, which complicates the use of conventional RNA interference (RNAi) approaches. These challenges are even more prominent in nondividing primary neurons, where transfection efficiency is inherently low. To address these limitations, this protocol outlines a lentiviral short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs)-based method for the efficient and specific depletion of eRNAs in primary cortical neurons. Step-by-step procedures are included for selecting shRNA target regions using nascent RNA sequencing data, generating shRNA-expressing lentiviruses, infecting primary neurons, and evaluating knockdown efficiency by RT-qPCR. This workflow offers a practical strategy for investigating eRNA function in postmitotic neurons and can be readily adapted to study enhancer-mediated transcriptional regulation in other nondividing cell types.

title: Role of Chromatin-Associated RNAs in Eye Physiology and Pathology.
abstract: Noncoding RNAs, including long noncoding RNAs, enhancer RNAs, circular RNAs, and small nuclear and nucleolar RNAs, represent a major, yet still largely uncharacterized, regulatory layer in the eye. A subset of these molecules, chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs), physically interacts with DNA and nuclear protein complexes to influence genome organization, transcriptional output, and stress responses. Although caRNAs have emerged as essential regulators of chromatin topology and gene expression in diverse tissues, their identity, dynamics, and mechanisms in the retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) remain elusive. Recent high-resolution genomic studies, disease transcriptomes, and mechanistic studies implicate dysregulated caRNAs in age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, and diabetic retinopathy, yet causal chromatin-level functions have rarely been demonstrated. In this review, we summarize current understanding of ncRNA-mediated regulation in vision, highlight emerging evidence for caRNA involvement in retinal development, photoreceptor and RPE specialization, and disease-associated epigenetic remodeling, and outline major mechanistic gaps that must be addressed. We then survey the rapidly expanding CRISPR toolbox, including base and prime editors, CRISPRi/a, Cas13 knockdown and editing platforms, and RNA-recruitment and spatial repositioning systems, that now enable targeted perturbation of both caRNA genomic loci and transcripts. These technologies provide the first practical route to move beyond correlative RNA-chromatin maps toward the mechanistic dissection of how caRNAs organize regulatory hubs, modulate enhancer-promoter communication, and shape long-range genome interactions in the eye. As the catalog of pathogenic noncoding variants grows, the ability to decode and engineer caRNA networks will be central to future precision therapeutic strategies for ocular disorders.

title: Astrocyte-enriched and cilia-related genetic signatures in dementia: A whole-exome sequencing study.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most prevalent form of dementia, is highly heritable, yet much of its genetic basis remains unexplained. Most genetic studies have focused on European populations, with limited data from under-represented groups. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) in the Han Chinese population may help identify novel rare variants and population-specific genetic risk factors. This study aims to use WES to identify potential candidate genes associated with dementia and AD in the Han Chinese population. In this exploratory pilot study, we performed WES in 63 Han Chinese patients with dementia, including 43 with AD and 20 with non-AD dementia (including one with dementia with Lewy bodies, one with Parkinson's dementia, four with frontotemporal dementia and 14 with mixed dementia), to identify rare coding variants. Gene-based case-control burden analyses using public gnomAD controls were conducted in the overall dementia cohort and the AD subgroup. Protein-protein interaction, functional enrichment, weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA) and gene set variation analysis (GSVA) using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets were performed to evaluate biological relevance and cell-type-specific activity. Cell-type marker enrichment analysis was used to identify relevant neuronal subtypes. Multilevel evidence was integrated to prioritise candidate risk genes. We identified suggestive rare variant signals in genes involved in cilia-related pathways, with stronger signals in the AD subgroup. These candidate genes were enriched in WGCNA modules associated with ageing, microtubule organisation and dementia pathology. GSVA showed increased activity of candidate genes in astrocytes using the snRNA-seq dataset. Cell-type marker analysis revealed strong enrichment in Ex6 excitatory neurons. Finally, integration of multilevel evidence prioritised 10 candidate genes. This pilot study provides preliminary evidence that cilia-related pathways may be involved in dementia, especially AD susceptibility in the Han Chinese population. Further validation in larger independent cohorts with ancestry-matched controls and in functional experiments is required. Larger sample sizes for each dementia subtype will improve the detection of both dementia-shared and subtype-specific signals.

title: Discovery and annotation of putative genes and novel RNA splice-isoforms in the human heart.
abstract: The analysis of long-read RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data can extend current annotations across the genomes, transcriptomes, and proteomes of even the most annotated species such as Homo sapiens. Long-read sequencing (LRS) technologies like Oxford Nanopore Technologies' (ONTs) nanopore sequencing can capture full-length transcripts, making the task of read-to-isoform assignment less challenging. This enables both the discovery of new RNA splice isoforms as well as a more accurate measure of their individual expression. RNA expression from unannotated regions of the genome can also lead to the discovery of putative (candidate novel) genes. Computational methods such as protein-coding potential assessment and ORF sequence prediction allow for the detection of new coding sequences (CDS), which can expand proteome annotations. This study seeks to apply these methods for the discovery of new RNA isoforms deriving from both annotated and putative genes in the human cardiac transcriptome. Recent LRS of prized Genotype Tissue Expression (GTEx) project human samples of the atrial appendage, left ventricle, and skeletal muscle were re-analysed with a new analytical pipeline that seeks to robustly discover these novel features. As a result, 54 intergenic and 112 antisense putative genes were detected. 491 novel RNA isoforms were discovered, 173 of which were transcribed from putative genes. 142 of the novel RNA isoforms were determined to have coding potential, and the remaining 349 determined to have limited or no coding potential with lengths greater than 200 nt, deeming them long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). Of the messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, 56 had low homology to known proteins, suggesting they may encode new protein isoforms or truncated proteins, and 24 had no detected homology to known proteins. Overall, this study has characterised new genes, RNA molecules, and protein isoforms, and has explored their potential function through various sequence and expression-based analyses, including the detection of conserved sequence and protein domains, cis-regulatory potential analysis, and weighted gene co-expression network analysis. Such analyses consistently demonstrated the potential for these discovered features to have functional roles in the human cardiac system. By re-analysing existing datasets, this study has revealed information that was not captured in previous analyses, resulting in more complete and accurate reference annotations of the human genome.

title: Regional tau burden tracks with lower microglial HLA class II transcription in the human brain.
abstract: Human leukocyte antigen class II (HLA-II) genes mark several microglial states in Alzheimer's disease, but it remains unclear how their average transcription relates to tau measured in the same brain region. We used a locked 13-gene HLA-II panel selected by biological function, cross-cohort detection, and variance, without considering effect estimates. The primary analysis was conducted using the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas (SEA-AD): 361 donor-region observations from 79 donors across 6 cortical regions were modeled with within-donor pathology decomposition, region fixed effects, and a donor random intercept. A paired entorhinal-versus-somatosensory analysis in GSE160936 (11 donors) provided additional support for our findings. Sensitivity analyses addressed amyloid-β, RNA quality, neuronal-nuclei enrichment, microglial-state composition, published state annotations, alternative panels, region omission, and assay modality. Public human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-microglia data were used to provide a distinct tau-exposure context. In the SEA-AD study, a higher local AT8-positive area within a donor was associated with a lower expanded HLA-II score (β = -0.174, 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.297 to -0.052; p = 0.005). The estimate remained negative after adjusting for local amyloid-β, RNA integrity number, and the NeuN-positive fluorescence-activated nuclei sorting (FANS) fraction (β = -0.167, 95% CI: -0.289 to -0.045; p = 0.007). This result was consistent after adjusting for the proportion of a published Damage-Associated Microglia (DAM)-enriched state. A formal tau-minus-amyloid-β contrast was not significant. In GSE160936, the expanded-panel pTau coefficient was negative (β = -0.533); however, the primary exact test was not significant after the two-test correction (p = 0.083; q = 0.166). Fibrillar tau exposure lowered the score derived from the 12 detectable panel genes in iPSC-microglia (difference = -1.343; exact p = 0.029). In a larger multi-region cohort and a smaller paired cohort, we observed that regional tau burden was associated with lower levels of pooled microglial HLA-II transcription. The association was not explained solely by the measured proportion of the DAM-like state. However, the data do not establish tau specificity, direct suppression, protein-level antigen presentation, or a causal mechanism.

title: NAT10-Mediated ac4C Modification of IRF7 Promotes Diabetic Nephropathy Progression.
abstract: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) progression involves pyroptosis. Interferon regulatory factor 7 (IRF7) can regulate pyroptosis, but its role in DN is unknown. The RNA modifier N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10) catalyses N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) and is linked to diabetic complications. This study tested whether NAT10-mediated ac4C modification of IRF7 mRNA exacerbates DN by promoting pyroptosis. The NAT10 expression levels in renal tissues from DN mice and in high-glucose (HG)-treated HK-2 cells were assessed by RT-qPCR and western blot. Cell viability, pyroptosis rate, levels of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-18) and expression of pyroptosis-related proteins (NLRP3, cleaved caspase-1, GSDMD-N) were evaluated by CCK-8 assay, flow cytometry, ELISA and western blot, respectively. The interaction between NAT10 and IRF7 mRNA was investigated through bioinformatics prediction, RIP, acRIP-qPCR and actinomycin D chase assays. In vivo, an AAV-mediated shRNA targeting NAT10 was delivered to DN mice. Renal function, histopathology, tissue inflammation and protein expression were analysed using biochemical assays, HE staining, ELISA, immunohistochemistry and western blot. NAT10 was upregulated in DN mice and HG-exposed HK-2 cells. Depletion of NAT10 inhibited HG-induced pyroptosis in HK-2 cells. Notably, NAT10 stabilized IRF7 through ac4C modification. Moreover, knockdown of NAT10 was found to alleviate HG-induced HK-2 cells' pyroptosis and DN in mice by downregulating IRF7 expression. NAT10 upregulation promotes DN progression by enhancing IRF7 mRNA stability through ac4C modification, which provides new therapeutic targets for DN treatment.

title: Long non-coding RNA LINC00657 aggravates atrial fibrosis in atrial fibrillation via the miR-144-3p/ROCK1 competing endogenous RNA axis.
abstract: The clinical significance and fibrogenic mechanisms of long non-coding RNA LINC00657 in atrial fibrillation (AF) remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate whether LINC00657 served as a mechanistic driver of atrial fibrogenesis in AF via modulation of the microRNA-144-3p (miR-144-3p)/Rho-associated coiled-coil containing protein kinase 1 (ROCK1) axis. LINC00657 expression was quantified in peripheral blood from 150 AF patients and 150 matched controls. Angiotensin II (Ang II)-stimulated primary rat cardiac fibroblasts and continuously infused C57BL/6 mice served as in vitro and in vivo fibrosis models, respectively. Functional assays (cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8), flow cytometry, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), western blot) and mechanistic experiments (subcellular fractionation, RNA pull-down, RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), dual-luciferase reporter) were conducted to dissect the LINC00657/miR-144-3p/ROCK1 competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) axis. Clinically, elevated circulating LINC00657 discriminated AF patients from controls and independently predicted AF risk, correlating positively with high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP). In vitro, Ang II induced LINC00657 upregulation; silencing LINC00657 suppressed cardiac fibroblast proliferation, attenuated the release of inflammatory cytokines interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), reduced the expression of fibrotic markers including type I/III collagen and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and promoted apoptosis. In vivo, knockdown of LINC00657 significantly attenuated Ang II-mediated atrial fibrosis in mice. Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring and transesophageal atrial pacing further revealed that silencing LINC00657 significantly restored the atrial effective refractory period (AERP) and markedly decreased both the inducibility and duration of AF. Mechanistically, LINC00657 was predominantly localized to the cytoplasm and functioned as a ceRNA to sponge miR-144-3p, with ROCK1 identified as a direct downstream target of miR-144-3p. Both AF patients and model mice exhibited decreased miR-144-3p and increased ROCK1 expression, which negatively and positively correlated with LINC00657 levels, respectively. Rescue experiments demonstrated that miR-144-3p inhibitors partially reversed the anti-fibrotic effects of LINC00657 silencing, whereas further ROCK1 knockdown abrogated this reversal. Mechanistically, dissection of ROCK1 downstream signaling revealed that the LINC00657/miR-144-3p/ROCK1 axis specifically activated the ROCK1/myosin light chain 2 phosphorylation pathway, enhancing actomyosin contractility and stress fiber formation to drive the fibrotic cascade. The LINC00657/miR-144-3p/ROCK1 regulatory axis contributed to atrial fibrosis in AF.

title: Primer: Orbiviruses.
abstract: Orbiviruses comprise numerous species and are transmitted by insect vectors. They are non-enveloped viruses with a multilayered capsid and a segmented double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) genome. Bluetongue virus (BTV), the prototype species of the genus Orbivirus, is a significant pathogen of livestock and is widely distributed throughout the world, causing serious periodic outbreaks with substantial economic consequences. Consequently, BTV has been extensively studied as a model orbivirus, resulting in a comprehensive understanding of its molecular epidemiology, genetics, biochemistry, structure, and replication cycle.
